speechtext: Mr. Speaker, hon. members on this side of the house are quite willing to fall in line with any suggestion the government may put forward with regard to the few days of recess at Easter. subtopic: AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just before the house adjourned yesterday I had dealt with the policy of the Conservative government in connection with the sale of wheat during their term of office. Previous to that I had dealt with the policy of the Liberal government prior to the last election. I dealt also with some of the suggestions put forward by hon. members of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation as to what the policy of the government should be in the marketing of wheat. Many criticisms have been made of the actions of the present board, one being that our wheat was put up

Wheat Board-Mr. Donnelly
at fire sale prices. I dealt partly with that criticism and for a few moments I intend to discuss more fully this so-called fire sale of our wheat.
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Per-ley) referred to a letter given to Mr. Lamont by the head of our wheat board when he was going over to England. It was a very fine letter and I recommend its being read by every hon. member. It is to be found on page 145 of the evidence given before the special committee on the marketing of wheat Which sat in 1936. It must be remembered that our wheat was not considered in a favourable light in England and that we had lost much of our market for wheat in that country. Yesterday I referred to the fact that we had lost many of the markets for our wheat, especially the market in England. The letter to which I refer was written by Mr. Murray and given to Mr. Lamont before he went to England in an endeavour to get back our market for wheat. I should like to read one or two paragraphs from that letter, as follows:
It is the desire of the board to permanently regain for Canadian wheat a full share of the import requirements of wheat in the British Isles and elsewhere. It is recognized by the board that a proper price relationship with other wheats must be maintained. With the good will of millers and consumers we feel that a better share of the available markets can be obtained for Canadian wheat.
I do not see anything wrong with that section; that is just what we were after. I continue:
You are authorized to assure the millers that in the event of their increasing the percentage of Manitobas in their flour blends that the policy of the board will be consistently that of making Canadian wheat available at fair competitive values. It is recognized by the board that the millers require, and must be given, assurance that when they do revert to the use of greater quantities of Canadian wheat in their flour blends that sufficient Canadian wheat will be constantly available to enable them to maintain the standard of the product supplied to their clientele of bakers and that no attempt will be made to hold them up in obtaining the needed supplies. The fixed minimum price paid producers by the board does not necessarily bear relationship to the board's selling price. Particular emphasis should be laid on regaining, through the British millers, the good will of the bakers for the use of a flour containing increased volume of Canadian wheat.
That is the very thing we were after. We wanted to get back the English market for our wheat which we had lost and which we had been losing for the past two or three years. The letter continues:
A fair premium should be considered what the millers of the world will pay for Canadian
wheat, based on its season-to-season value compared with other wheats, and allowing for the free use of Canadian wheat in volume.
The principal reason the board are sending you to England is to cultivate the cooperation and good will of British millers towards the use of Canadian wheat.
I think anyone who reads that letter must come to the conclusion that that was the very thing that needed to be done. Under the conditions that existed then, I think the letter was well prepared and very well written. There is no suggestion in it that our wheat was going to be sold at prices which were not competitive with other world prices. We did regain our markets and we did sell our wheat. There is no doubt that this letter written to Mr. Lamont, and the other letter sent to the British millers, which will be found in the same place in the evidence, indicating to them that we were intending to compete with other wheats of the world, and that we would do everything we possibly could to see that they got our wheat at fair competitive prices, did much to get back for us the market in the British Isles which we had lost.
Another criticism in connection with this matter has to do with the amount of money which the western farmers are said to have lost because of the fact that the price of wheat went up last year. I listened to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Cold-well) sav that he had told people last year that the price of wheat was going up to S1.25-at all events he said it was reported in the press and that the report was correct. I wish I could have been sure that the price was going up to S1.25 last year; had I known that I would have made some money. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle says:	"They
were so certain in Winnipeg that the price of wheat would go up that you did not even have to put up any hedges; the banks allowed you to buy wheat without having any money at all. Just think of having an opportunity like that knowing that the price of wheat was going up and knowing that you could get all the money you wanted for nothing. Why, a man could be a millionaire-that is, a man who had brains enough to get into this house should have been a millionaire. I should like to ask the hon. member for Qu'Appelle how much money he made. Surely he made a lot. I am not much impressed with the remarks of a man who relies on the course of the markets, whether the stock market or the wheat market, for his political arguments. How can he tell what is going to happen? I wish someone could tell me what the price of wheat will be next fall.

speechtext:
Or to-morrow.

Wheat Board.-Mr. Donnelly

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, or to-morrow. I should like to get into the market if I could tell what the price of wheat will be next October. I wonder whether those who prophesy these prices are ready to back their opinion with their money.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Or with their wheat.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If they are not, I do not think much of their predictions. There is one sure way for a man to show that he is sure of a thing, and that is by spending his-money to prove it. As the saying is, if our foresight were only as good as our hindsight, we would be all right. A lot of us would like to be in that position.
I should like to say a word or two with regard to a criticism made by the horn, member for Rosetown-Biggar. He said yesterday:
Mr. James R. Murray had lost the confidence of the great mass of the producers in western Canada. They did not feel like delivering to a board headed by Mr. Murray.
All I want to say in that regard is that any man who sat on the committee last year and listened to Mr. James Murray giving evidence must have been convinced, if he knew anything about the grain trade, that Mr. Murray knew his business, that he was a capable man and that he was the right man to do the job that he was doing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And an honest public servant.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not only that, but a man who had. supported the wheat pool policy- who was one of the first to advocate it and still supports it.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And drafted the contract.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If we had had a man like Mr. James Murray at the head of the wheat pools when they were started, it is my firm belief that they would be operating successfully yet. What was wrong with our pools was that we did not have at the head of them a man who knew his business, who knew how to carry them on. That is why they went broke; that is why they are in the position they are in to-day. If there is any truth at all in the suggestion that Mr. Murray has lost the confidence of the producers, it must be because there are cheap politicians going around among the farmers and abusing Murray, saying that he does not understand his job and is trying to work against their interests.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, speaking here yesterday, referring to the Tur-geon commission, also said:
The government, I think, made a grave error when they appointed Colonel Ralston as counsel for that commission.
fMr. J. G. Ross.l
I am not going to say anything about the compensation that is paid Colonel Ralston, but I will say that I sat for three years on the committee which investigated the mixing of wheat, and I know we tried to get the services of a counsel to write amendments to the grain act: we had the greatest trouble in obtaining one who understood the grain act and the wheat business well enough to rewrite the statute in its present form. We practically had to dictate the terms which our counsel was required to write into the act, and to amend and reamend the draft in order to get it right. I repeat that it is one of the hardest things imaginable to find an unattached lawyer who is fully conversant with the workings of the act. We could, I suppose, have got lawyers who were tied up with the Winnipeg Grain Exchange, but what a howl would have gone up from western Canada if we had asked them to assist us. It would have been said, "We know now what we are going to get; we shall get a report in favour of the grain exchange."
'Another point to be borne in mind is that wheat marketing is a national problem, not one confined to western Canada. Only last year the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) said in the committee that the greatest problem with which we had to deal was that of marketing wheat, that it was as important as our railway problem. I remember remarking at the time that I thought the growing of wheat was just as great a problem as the marketing of it. But I agree that marketing is of national importance; and we wanted to engage someone in whom eastern as well as western Canada would have confidence. That can be said of Colonel Ralston. He is an able man; he knows wheat, and he knows the grain act as well as any man in eastern Canada. I was astonished at the knowledge he displayed both of the law and of the handling of wheat.
Having dealt with some past criticisms. I will refer briefly to what happened at the las* session of the house. At that time the leader of the opposition criticized the chairman of the wheat board and laid certain charges against him. The government saw fit to appoint a special committee to deal with those charges and also to study the best ways of marketing wheat. That committee sat and looked into the various charges that were made against the head of the wheat board. After the hearing of witnesses a report was drawn up with reference to those charges. I remember that the adoption of that report was moved by the man who made the charges, namely, the leader of the opposition, so that he must have been satisfied that his accusations against Mr. Murray had not been proved.

Wheat Board-Mr. Leader
With regard to the marketing of wheat, we as a committee did not feel that we were in a position to investigate and bring in a report as to the best method. We came to that decision for several reasons. We could not go to England, to Australia, to the Argentine and elsewhere to examine the systems in operation there and decide whether they were applicable to our Canadian situation. Another reason was found in the constitution of the committee. Some of its members, being Liberals, believed in the Liberal policy of marketing wheat: "Let the world know we have wheat to sell at a fair price." Others, who belonged to the Conservative party, apparently thought the best way to sell was: " Set a price and make the world pay that price before they can get our wheat." Also on the committee were some of our Cooperative Commonwealth Federation friends, who suggested, " Let us take over all elevators and boats and the marketing of our wheat all over the world, and let us have our agents who will carry on that marketing business." I presume it would be a socialistic form of marketing wheat. There were those who believed in a one hundred per cent pool, those who believed in a compulsory pool, and those who believed in the open marketing of wheat. With all these divergent views it was impossible for us to come to a definite decision, and we therefore suggested that a royal commission should be appointed to look into the whole matter, and advised the government accordingly. A commission was then appointed, in the person of Mr. Justice Turgeon, and the investigation is still in progress. I held, and I am still of the opinion, that the government made a mistake when it altered the marketing of wheat in the absence of a report from that commission. I submit that the board should have been allowed to function until such time as the commission brought in its report. I do not think that the price of wheat should have been raised until that time. The minimum payment, or whatever you choose to call it, was 874 cents and it should have remained at that level until the submission of the report by the royal commission. I do not believe that the marketing of wheat as it was carried on under that board should have been changed in any respect until the commission gave its report. I may be wrong, but that is the view I expressed at home before coming here and it is the view I hold now.
The amendment which has been moved" to the motion before the house expresses regret that the government rendered the Canadian Wheat Board Act of 1935 inoperative in its application to the 1936 wheat crop. So far as that is concerned, I suggest that the
wheat board was not altogether inactive; at any rate its inactivity with regard to the 1936 crop helped the farmers of the west. It helped in the marketing of the 1936 crop because when the crop began to come on the market the wheat board did not press for sale of the old crop which it had on its hands. In that way it kept the 1936 crop from becoming a burden on the market and forcing prices down. For a considerable time the wheat board refrained from selling wheat and therefore did help in the marketing of the 1936 crop.
If I were in the house-I do not expect to be here when the vote is taken-I should feel obliged to vote for the amendment. I will saj' this, however. As far as this motion is concerned, it does not represent, to me at any rate, a loss of confidence in the government. I still have confidence in the government and I believe that it will do what is right with lespect to many other matters. This particular question may be one of the things in respect to which I differ from the government, but that is to be expected in human affairs. People are apt to differ in many ways but in this respect only do I differ from the government so far as its wheat policy is concerned.
M r. HARR\ LEADER (Portage la Prairie): In rising to speak to the question before the house I intend to be as brief as possible having regard to the importance of the subject. By way of introduction I may observe that I have been a producer of wheat all my life and therefore I should know something about the production end of the business. And having operated a public elevator and bought and sold wheat in the grain trade I think I should know something of the selling end of it. In addition to that I was selected as a member of the special committee last year which inquired into the marketing of wheat. But what is of more importance to me is that this is a vital question to my constituents.
I believe it was the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) who pointed out yesterday that there had been altogether too much politics in connection with the markets ing of wheat. With that statement I heartily agree. Wheat is the most important food of all the nations of the world and is the very lifeblood of the farmers of western Canada. It seems to me therefore that we should get away from the political aspect in the marketing of wheat and try to get together to see if we cannot decide on a policjf which will be in the interests not only of the wheat producers but of all the people of Canada. I regret therefore that there is a political side to this great question.

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext:
Wheat Board-Mr. Leader
I suggest however that politics is not altogether confined to one party; I believe we have it more or less in all parties. In my opinion the Conservatives have seized upon this opportunity to make political capital out of the wheat question and they must be content if we judge them by their actions when they had responsibility. It is quite easy to offer criticism when you have no responsibility, and that is what has been done by my genial friend for whom I have much respect, the hon. member for Qu'-Appelle (Mr. Perley).
Politicians have the inclination when they have not the opportunity, and very often when they have the opportunity they have not the inclination. When I was out on the farm a few years ago I wondered why our government had not made an attempt to get our money on a parity with the English pound. Britain was our market; that was where we had to sell our products; and in 1932 when the price of wheat reached the lowest point on the Liverpool market in over 400 years; and when it was selling in Fort William at a little over 38 cents per bushel, we were selling that wheat in the markets of Great Britain when the English pound was worth only $3.60 compared with a normal value of almost $5-$4.86 and a fraction to be exact. That was a serious handicap and the result was a very small price for our farm products. It struck me at that time that something should be done, and I remember picking up our family bible, which was the Winnipeg Free Press, in which I noticed on the financial page a double column article giving a speech made by Senator Sharpe in the Senate of Canada. The remarks reported in that article were made by a supporter of the then Conservative government, and they were interesting to me because it is so unusual for the supporter of a government to criticize the powers that be. I should like to read an extract from Senator Sharpe's speech. It will be found in the debates of the senate of November 24, 1932 at page 178:
I cannot believe that the Prime Minister understands the real condition of the people. Our farmers are facing ruin because of the disparity between buying and selling prices. The British pound is now at $3.60, a discount of 25 per cent.	If we went off the gold
standard and brought our currency to the level of the British pound the result undoubtedly would be an increase of from 12 cents to 15 cents a bushel in the price of wheat; we should get $20 more for a 1,200 pound steer, and butter, cheese, eggs, pork and all other farm products would command higher figures. Virtually all our important competitors in agricultural products throughout the world, except the United States, have gone off the gold standard.

I believe it was the following year that President Roosevelt of the United States decided to desert the gold standard, and thereby Canada's money was brought to a parity with the British pound. But it was only through the action of the President of the United States that this came about. Judging by events taking place at that time, if the Conservative party were in power in Canada at the present time the British pound would still be worth only $3.60 to the Canadian producer.
Senator Sharpe went on to say:
If we were tied up to the British pound-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must remind the hon. member that it is not permitted to quote here a speech made in another house.

Well, I shall abide by the
rules, but I am sorry, because it is very interesting.
Quote the Free Press.

Was it not made outside
of the senate?

With this reference I will
conclude. Senator Sharpe declared, according to the Free Press report, that $125,000,000 was lost to the producers in Canada in 1932 in selling their products on the British market on account of the difference in exchange.
I am sorry that the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) is not in his seat to-day; he was prime minister at the time. I am sure he would agree it is a fair statement that he did not place our money on a par with the British pound because he thought it would ruin Canada's credit, and as usual the farmers of western Canada paid the price.
I want to compare the actions of the former wheat board under Mr. McFarland with the actions under the present manager, Mr. Murray. Mr. McFarland's policy was to stabilize the market, to hold for a higher price. I cannot understand his attitude in view of the experience we had under the pooling system, because that is exactly what the pool did, and it proved disastrous. Our customers were not going to pay any more than they had to, and to hold a gun to the head of our best customer, demanding a higher price, was a disastrous policy. That, however, is exactly what the pool did, and Mr. McFarland, after all that experience, adopted the same policy. When Mr. Murray was made manager of the wheat board he adopted the opposite policy; he assured our customers that there was Canadian wheat for sale every day at the market price. Thus he won their confidence. Between the two I have no hesitation in saying that Mr. Murray's policy is the better.

Wheat Board-Mr. Leader
The fact that he sold that huge surplus is the greatest factor in the better price prevailing at the present time. There are other factors I know, but buyers know that Canada has got rid of that huge surplus and it will not come into competition with the crop that we hope to produce this year.
It seems to me that the present wheat board is going out of business. I can come to no other conclusion. But the farmers of western Canada are not going to give up the fight they have made for twenty-five years for a better marketing policy, and if this wheat board goes out of business something else will have to take its place. I made that statement in Winnipeg this year at the annual meeting of the pool elevator companies of Manitoba. They asked me to say something and I did so very hesitantly, because at that time the government was not in very good repute with the Manitoba pool elevator companies. I spoke of course without assuming any responsibility except for myself. I said that I believed the government's action was wrong, that I felt that the wheat board was going out of business and that we should rebuild on the foundations of the old wheat pool another selling agency. I told them that we have in Canada two farmer organizations dealing in wheat, the pool elevator companies and the United Grain Growers' Grain Company. The latter company, although owned by the farmers, is a commercial institution pure and simple, yet it is regarded by the people of eastern Canada as a farmers' organization; therefore they say to us: You people in western Canada do not know what you want; you have got two farmer organizations out there and cannot agree among yourselves; there is cutthroat competition. And it is the truth. I suggested that the United Grain Growers' Grain Company and the western pool elevator companies get together and prove to eastern Canada and to ourselves that we have a policy, that we can cooperate to sell our products on the world markets, assuring our customers that we have a good product for sale and are willing to sell it at the market price. I took the same attitude at the convention of the United Farmers of Manitoba at Neepawa. I told them the same story and I am telling it to the house to-day, because I want the house to know that I am consistent. At their annual meeting held in Calgary on January 20 the United Farmers of Alberta instructed their executive to study the possibility of a merger between the pool elevator system and the Grain Growers' Grain Company.
There has been a good deal said in regard to resolutions passed at meetings of farmers
in the west. Some of the resolutions referred to were stereotyped, some were different, some could not be vouched for, others were suspicious, and they were rather up in the air in general. But I hold in my hand a resolution passed at the convention of the United Farmers of Manitoba at Neepawa last fall, which I should like to read to the house:
Wheat marketing: In considering the matter of wheat marketing we discover a very wide spread for opportunity to market western wheat under a dominion grain board. This view, which prevailed almost if not quite unanimously among our delegates, is expressed in the following resolution:
Whereas the opinion prevails almost universally among producers of grain that the operations of a grain board in Canada may prove in future of very great practical value;
And whereas we are convinced that the grain board should operate regardless of the market price of wheat;
Therefore the United Farmers of Manitoba puts itself on record as urging that the wheat board set up last year be retained in operation, that it function independently of the figure at which the market price stands, and that thus there be secured to the farmers the privilege of placing their wheat with the board at any time.
That is the resolution passed by men and women who are engaged in this business of producing wheat. I was present at the convention and I voted for the resolution.
The government must take full responsibility for their action in changing the Canadian Wheat Board Act. They did not consult me, therefore I have to make my stand clear. I intend to support the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle. The amendment is regarded by some as a vote of want of confidence in the government. I do not regard it as such. I still have confidence in the government, but I do not believe in the course they took in regard to this measure. I do not believe it was justified; I do not believe it was in the best interests of my constituents, and Mr. Speaker, my constituents come first.

Mr. Speaker, as I understand the question as it has been placed before the house by a member of the official opposition, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley), the action of the government is being criticized because it is said to be legally unsound. The right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), who I suppose speaks for the opposition, concluded his remarks with this statement, appearing at page 1870 of Hansard:
The real issue is whether hon. members are prepared to stand in their places and say that they approve of the executive making a statute inoperative when there is no power or authority so to do.
Wheat Board-Mr. Tucker

I presume we may take it that the right hon. gentleman was speaking of the true intent of this motion, so in effect he said that anyone who voted for this motion would be declaring that the government acted illegally in the course it took; that it is not a question of whether the government's action was right or wrong or whether or not it was justified. The straight charge is made that the government had no power to do what it did, and this parliament is asked to criticize the government for that reason.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.

If that is the issue upon which we must vote, every hon. member should carefully consider the situation, and I have endeavoured to do so. I must admit that when I heard the first report of the government's action I was inclined to take the position that the government had no legal power to do what they did. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, even to-day I am inclined to doubt whether they had such legal power, but I am prepared to take this position: I recognize that in this house we have in the person of the right hon. leader of the opposition a lawyer of very high standing in this country, and that his opinion is entitled to a great deal of consideration and respect. I also realize, however, that advising the government we have a lawyer of equal standing in the country whose opinion is entitled to the same consideration and respect. I refer to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), and I take it that he advised the government in this matter. I have no doubt that the government would not have taken this action if they had not been advised by the Minister of Justice and the law officers of the crown that they had a legal right to do so.
Faced with that situation, with the leader of the opposition giving it as his opinion that the government had no legal right to take that action, and with the opinion which I must assume has been given by the Minister of Justice that the government had a legal right to take the course that was taken, what am I -to do, as an ordinary and rather young member of the legal profession sitting in this house? I must bear in mind the debates which took place in connection with the so-called new deal legislation of the last administration, which I followed closely. At that time the present right hon. leader of the opposition was positive that the legislation he was introducing was intra vires of this parliament and so would receive the approval of the judicial committee of the privy council. At the same time the present Minister of Justice was very doubtful whether

those acts were within the power of this parliament. What was the opinion of the highest judicial authority in the British Empire? Right along in its decisions as to whether those acts were intra vires or not it upheld the opinion of the Minister of Justice as against that of the right hon. leader of the opposition. How does that affect me in judging which opinion, in the present case, is likely to be upheld by the highest court of this empire? I must say that under the circumstances I am forced to take the position that, until something different has been proved, I can follow the opinion of the Minister of Justice with more confidence than that of the leader of the opposition.
But there is something else I think should be mentioned as well. We know that the wheat pool of western Canada has become a powerful organization, retaining some of the best lawyers in the west. We know that the suggestion was made at once tliat the government had no legal power to pass the order in council in question. I confidently expected that if the wheat pool held that opinion they would immediately challenge the action of the government in the courts, as they had a right to do. They could have brought an action or made application for a mandamus forcing the wheat board to accept wheat as they alleged it was required to do under the wheat board act. I waited, confidently expecting the pool to back up their statements by an action to test the validity of their opinion. After all, Mr. Speaker, we who are lawyers are hesitant about being over sure as to the interpretation of a statute. We are inclined to let the courts express opinions rather than state our own with too much certainty ahead of time and1, as I say, I confidently expected that the position of the government would be challenged in the courts at once. I waited day after day and week after week, but when the most powerful organization in western Canada which was vitally interested in the matter, did not see fit to resort to the courts I must confess in all sincerity that I began to have doubts as to the soundness of my own opinion that the government had acted without legal authority.
That is my position. At the time the government made this decision I thought they had acted without legal authority, as the leader of the opposition said. When no action was taken by the wheat pool I began to have my doubts. Then when I -thought the situation over and considered the history of the two men whose opinions I should value, I had further doubts, so that I am in this position: I am asked

Wheat Board-Mr. Tucker
by the official opposition to vote against the government because they did something without legal authority, illegally, but to-day the whole matter is in doubt. No one can say with any assurance that the action was legal or illegal, so in effect the official opposition want the members of this house to vote against the government before they have proved their case.
That is the legal point of view, and 1 think that is a fair attitude to take. If they want us to find the government guilty, let them prove their case. Unsupported statements are not sufficient before a court of law, and they should not be sufficient before this parliament. That is the bare legal ground, and the right hon. leader of the opposition has placed the matter on that ground. I do not think that is altogether sufficient for this house, however, and for a few moments I should like to refer to the effect of this amendment. What was the proper thing for the government to do last fall. Well, the question may be considered from many angles, but this was my attitude: Having set up a royal commission to investigate the whole question I felt that the government should not have made any change in the operation of the act until that commission had reported. But there was another point to be considered. Every farmer in western Canada, especially those who believed in cooperation, wanted to see the wheat board get a fair chance. Would the wheat board have had a fair chance if the initial price had been set at 874 cents a bushel? I noticed that the hon. gentleman who introduced this amendment did not mention what initial price he would have liked the government to set. I take it that he would have liked the government to continue the wheat board, setting the initial price at 87J cents. He has not said differently; the official opposition have not said differently, so I take it that is their attitude.
What would have been the effect if that had been done? Well, the other night the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) in effect said this: Considering the attitude of those who believed in the wheat board and who wanted it to have a fair trial, we realized that if we had continued the wheat board as in the previous year and set a price of 874 cents, very few people would have delivered wheat to the board. There is no doubt about that being correct, because the price on the open market was very much higher than 874 cents. Very few people would have delivered to the wheat board. The expenses of running the wheat board would have come out of the small amount of wheat delivered to
it. Those who wished to destroy the board would have been able to come to parliament the following session and say the people in western Canada do not want the wheat board because they did not deliver to it, and therefore we should do away with it. The question is this: Who is the greater friend of the wheat board, the man who is ready to give it a chance or the man who pretends to give it a chance, under conditions that he knows will cause it to be destroyed? That is something for the people of Canada to consider.
We have to be fair about this matter. I heard someone say-not loudly, but I was just able to hear it-
I will say it loudly.
I hoped the hon. member would.
In setting a ninety cent conditional figure a situation was created under which absolutely no wheat would be delivered to the board. They had no opportunity, even if they so desired.

That is just my point. The government prevented a situation developing whereby the farmers would have had the right to deliver to the wheat board, knowing that they would not do so as would have been the case if the price were left at the old figure of 874 cents. Very few would have done it. The figures were given by the Minister of Agriculture. In the time they could have delivered to the wheat board,
38.000.000 bushels were marketed and only
600,000	bushels were actually delivered to the board.
Then we have the proof from the people who should know most about it, namely the wheat pools themselves. What is their opinion about it? I should like to place it before the house, because we want to be fair. This is the considered statement of the executives of the three Canadian wheat pools, as issued on July 6. Here is what they said:
If the minimum price for wheat is set below the futures market price, the Canadian wheat board might be crippled, if not destroyed-
Is that what my hon. friend wants?
-as farmers after the experience of the present crop year would be reluctant to deliver their wheat to the board if they could secure a higher price on the open market.
That is the opinion of the wheat pool officials themselves. They believed that if the government had permitted delivery to the wheat board at an initial price of 874 cents it might have destroyed the wheat
Wheat Board-Mr. Tucker

board. Will anybody stand here and vote for that sort of thing, while pretending he is supporting the wheat board and the wheat board idea?
But I am asked, " What attitude did you take in the country "? My answer is that I tried to take the attitude in the country that I thought was the right one. The proper idea, it seemed to me, should be for the present to continue the wheat board in operation. The only chance in the world it had to get a fair trial was to set its price sufficiently high that the farmer would feel able to deliver to it. I advocated that the initial price should be $1.01, which was slightly under the existing market price at that time. I figured that on that basis .the farmer would deliver in reasonable quantities to the wheat board, and in that way the board would be given a fair chance. Again, on that basis, it seemed to me, the government would not stand to lose much. I hoped the government would take that attitude, and made representations accordingly. They decided, however, not to take that stand-and mind you, Mr. Speaker, if they did not see fit to set the price high enough to give the wheat board a chance, it was better to take the attitude they did take. Anybody who says he prefers to see the wheat board continue, while setting a price of 87J cents, is voting for something which in the words of the wheat pool officials themselves, might have killed the wheat board. I tried to take a consistent attitude. I said the price should be set high enough so that the wheat board should have a chance, and made representations accordingly. Wheu the government decided it would not do that I expressed my disappointment. If that is a crime, if it is a crime to say one is disappointed in the attitude of a government on a specific question, then I am guilty of it. But-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a virtue.

Probably I have been guilty of it more than once. However, to say that I am disappointed in some action of the government, and to say it not only to the country but on the floor of the house, is entirely different from saying that I am going to vote lack of confidence in the government. Ever since there has been a Liberal government in Canada and ever since I have taken an interest in public affairs, I would have liked to see those Liberal governments cut the tariff to a point a good deal lower than it was at the moment. But government in Canada is a matter of compromise. Just because it does not go as far as one would like to see it go. should one throw out people who are going farthest in your direction in order 
to bring in others who will not go any distance in your direction? That is the question one must answer.
Or will go in the wrong direction.
Yes. The hon. member is certainly not referring to the Liberal party when he makes that observation.
He would not admit it if he were.

In regard to the attitude taken that we might have lost some money, may I say, in passing, and by way of putting myself on record, that I think no harm would have been done by setting the price at $1.01. That is only my opinion. In justice to the western farmers I feel a reasonable price should be fixed or ensured for our wheat production. It is my view that when western Canada has come through such hard times and has suffered a succession of crop failures or poor crops that last year the government might very well have set an initial price at $1.01, so that those farmers who wished so to do could have delivered to the wheat board and obtained some benefit from any subsequent rise in price.
In that connection however there is something I should like to draw to the attention of hon. members. There seems to be the idea that if the wheat board had been permitted to operate, the grain exchange or the grain dealers would not have got the wheat delivered to the wheat board. May I invite your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the fact that one of the first things Mr. McFarland did, as head of the wheat authority set up by the last administration, was to force the pools to close their direct selling agencies in Europe and to deal through that very grain exchange, through the established selling agencies. And so last year, had the wheat board been taking the delivery of wheat from the 1936 crop, under the specific direction of the last parliament in the wheat board act, that wheat would have had to be sold through established channels to the grain trader members of the grain exchange, and the grain exchange would have got just as much of it as it has already got. That is something which should not be overlooked.
Then, suppose wheat had been delivered to the wheat board: under that condition they would have had to turn round and sell it on the grain exchange through established channels. What would have been the effect? They were supposed to sell their wheat in an orderly fashion. The members of the grain exchange would have been able to buy it up

Wheat Board-Mr. Tucker
and if they had thereby gambled successfully they would have made their half million dollars which the leader of the opposition mentioned the other day. The only thing was that it would have gone from the farmer to the wheat board and from it to the grain exchange, instead of direct from the farmer to the grain exchange. Is that something to raise an issue about? Is there much difference in that? I am asking hon. members that question.
Then, there is the question whether or not the farmers of western Canada, the primary producers, are entitled to some consideration under our present economic set-up. The hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross) gives it as his opinion that the farmers in western [DOT]Canada are entitled to no subsidy, no protection. nothing of that sort. I would say to him that if it were within the realm of prac-ical politics to do away with tariffs and subsidies, then the wheat farmer of western Canada would have to take his chance with the Test and would be willing to do so. But who in parliament will say that to-day that is within the realm of practical politics? Who will stand in his place and say there is any chance of our doing away with tariffs, within the lifetime of any hon. member? We know "that a certain measure of protection for the secondary industries of this country is a permanent part of our fiscal set-up. It has not been quite so high under the Liberals as :it has been under the Tories, thank goodness. I pointed out recently that in 1931 in one year the tariff subsidies had cost the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta a total of $54,925,000. If that should be taken as a normal year, in six years the cost to the three prairie provinces of tariff subsidies to protect our secondary industries would total $329,552,000. Through failure to place our money on the same basis as Australia during those years the prairie provinces lost another $229,000,000 in the selling price of their wheat alone, so that the total loss to western Canada under these items was $558,000,000. Then somebody says that the western farmer is not entitled to a fixed price ifor his wheat, sufficient to ensure him a fair standard of living which might cost the government half a million, a million or even ten million dollars. That is the situation as it appears to a lot of people in western Canada and as it appears to myself. I say: Go as far as you can in lowering tariffs, go as far as our party is willing to go-goodness knows I should like to see them go farther than they have gone yet-and when you have gone that [DOT]far, in justice to those who are engaged in
our primary industries, give them some compensation for the loss they suffer because of that tariff policy. That is only just.
We are asked to vote non-confidence in the government. Is it better for the farmers to have wheat selling at $1.31 with marketing machinery not quite as perfect as it might be, than to have the price forced down to 50 cents per bushel through your trade policies and have the most wonderful marketing machinery that could be devised by the mind of man? We are asked to vote non-confidence in this Liberal government, but what is the record? I predicted in 1930 at more than one of the election campaign meetings that if the Tory government got into power and carried out its tariff policies, there would be reprisals, quotas and so on on the part of countries with which we refused to trade. I told my listeners that as a natural result wheat would pile up in this country until the price dropped to 25 cents a bushel. I was fortunate, or perhaps lucky, in 1935 when I again made a prediction that has already almost come true that if the Liberal party came into power and the tariff was lowered so that we could sell our wheat in the markets of the world, inside of two years wheat would be back to $1.25 per bushel. What does the record show?
In 1926 there was grown in this country
407.000.	000 bushels of wheat, in round figures. In 1927 the crop totalled 479,000.000 bushels and in 1928, 566,000,000 bushels. What was the carry-over after such large crops? On July 31, 1929, the carry-over was only 104,-
383,000	bushels. In 1929 the crop totalled
304.520,000	bushels. In four years while the Liberals were in office there was a crop of
1.758.000.	000 bushels. The carry-over on July 31. 1930, was just 111,094.000 bushels. What is the history of the time the Conservative government was in power? We find that in 1931 the crop totalled 321,000.000 bushels, in round figures. In 1932 it totalled 443,000,000 bushels; in 1933, 281,000,000 bushels, and in 1934, 275,000.000 bushels. In other words, in 1931 to 1934 inclusive the total crop of wheat amounted to 1,322.000,000 bushels. Even with those comparatively small crops the carryover had increased to 203,000,000 bushels as at July 31. 1935. During these four years of Conservative administration there was 449,000,000 bushels less wheat grown in this country than the four years of Liberal administration, but the carry-over had increased by
92.000.	000 bushels. Can anyone say that there is nothing in trade policies? What was the result? Prices responded accordingly. If enormous carry-overs are built up in this country, the inevitable result is that prices
Wheat Board-Mr. Tucker

go down. When your trade policy is such that you can get rid of that carry-over and continue to show signs of getting rid of it year after year, prices go up.
This brings me to the last step. Is it not better for the farmers of this country when they do grow a crop to be able to get well over a dollar a bushel than to have a perfect wheat board operating and get only 35 or 40 cents a bushel? We have to get down to fundamentals. What is the situation? When the government announced its policy last year I suggested to some members of the wheat pool directorate that the pool was set up to carry on cooperative marketing. I told them that in the past they had been hampered due to the fact that when they wanted to make an initial payment they had to go to the banks to borrow the money and the banks insisted that they hedge their wheat. The purpose they had in mind, that of orderly marketing, was thus defeated. I told them that with the policy of this government of guaranteeing 874 cents a bushel they could establish at once a voluntary pool and offer the farmers 80 cents a bushel as an initial payment. I -told them they would not need to hedge their wheat, that they could once more get their pool going and if it was destined to be the success it should be, if they had confidence in it themselves now was the time to start it under such favourable circumstances, they would then have one year of successful marketing operations to take before the Turgeon grain commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They were guaranteed against loss.

As the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) says, they were guaranteed against loss. That was a golden opportunity for the wheat pools of this country if they had seen their way clear to take advantage of it. With all due deference to eastern members, I must say that I have more confidence in western people when it comes to handling our wheat. It is their own work and they should know it intimately. I feel they are better able to do that than any grain board which might be appointed by the government. After all a grain board appointed by the national government would have to consider questions affecting eastern Canada as well as western Canada. It seems to me that we should try to handle our own business as much as possible. People might be placed upon that wheat board who would not be satisfactory to western Canada. I suggested that under the pool system they could see to it that the men they wanted were appointed.

They could appoint whom they liked and they would thereby have control over their own business. They had their opportunity. That was laid before the wheat pools and their first answer was that they did not have time to set it in motion. There might have been something in that argument; it is unfortunate that the decision of the government was not made sooner. However on the basis of the government's decision, the other grain handling concerns in western Canada said to anybody who wanted to deliver wheat to them, " We will give you an advance of 80 cents per bushel on your wheat." I think the wheat pools should have been able to do just the same as these other grain marketing organizations. They are just as well organized and just as ably managed. But they also gave another reason. They said in effect, " We have been fighting for a wheat board, and if we start a voluntary pool going again it will be more or less an admission that we do not stand firmly for a wheat board." In that regard, I think, the executive of the wheat pool did not represent the real wishes of their people. Their members believe in cooperative marketing, not in state socialism. That is where this house is perhaps split. Do you believe in cooperation, in people handling their own business, or do you believe in placing it in the hands of the government and asking them to handle it for you? That is the situation.
I may have disagreed with things the government did at the time. But while I might disagree for the moment with some step that was taken, I believe they are moving in the right direction. I believe that there is a great opportunity, upon the basis of the policy the government have pursued so far, of setting cooperation in motion again. I hope the government will again guarantee a price during the coming crop year, so that the pool will have another opportunity to commence again the pooling of wheat and that the policy will be announced at an early enough date that it, will not have to be said again that there is not time to get it in motion to handle this year's crop.
In conclusion, I am inclined perhaps more than some other members are to speak out, to criticize, when I do not agree with something. But there is this to be remembered. A man may give his whole life to the service of the people; he may be right ninety-nine times out of one hundred, but let him make one mistake and people will sometimes pay more attention to the one mistake than to the ninety-nine times he was right. That is a tendency which has caused many people to refuse to have anything to do with public life. This I bear

Wheat Board-Mr. Dunning
in mind when considering the attitude I should take towards the present government: while there are certain directions in which I should like them to go further than they have; while sometimes I have not agreed with all they have done, I think they are moving a good deal further in the direction I would have them go than would conceivably be the case with the official opposition that moved this amendment, and so I have no hesitation in saying that I intend to vote against the amendment and to vote confidence in the present Liberal government.
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance): Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to impede the passing of the motion that you, Mr. Speaker, do leave the chair; therefore I shall be brief. I am anxious to get along with the business of the ways and means committee. My task is rendered easier by the remarks of the hon. member for Rosthem (Mr. Tucker) to which we have just listened, because he developed a number of the points which I had it in mind to make.
First, I should like to point out that the address of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) on the amendment the other day did not call in question in the slightest degree the wisdom of the government's policy; it merely called in question the legality of the government's action. As to that legality, the hon. member for Rosthern has developed the obvious legal answer. I can only say on behalf of the government that in legal matters we are and must be guided by the opinion of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) and the law officers of the crown, and with respect to the legality of the course taken there is no doubt whatever in the mind either of the Minister of Justice or of the law officers. I know, of course, that the leader of the opposition dealt with the legality, leaving it to his colleague the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) to speak with respect to the advisability. The reason is apparent. The leader of a great national party could not make an address having to do with the affairs of merely a section of the country from the standpoint of the advisability of the policy. He had to approach it on some broad, national ground, and the only such ground available to him was that of legality. However, he left the hon. member for Qu'Appelle and others quite free to develop their own sectional arguments with respect to the advisability of the policy followed, and of course the gentlemen concerned have done so.
I am not going to evade in the slightest degree the question of the soundness of the policy followed by the government; I am prepared to meet the issue of the soundness

of the policy at the time it was determined. In saying that, Mr. Speaker, I feel conscious of my limitations. I am not a wheat expert like the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) and some of the other hon. members who have spoken. I have only been dealing with wheat, growing it, buying it and selling it long enough to be sure of one thing, and that is that the man who projects his course upon an opinion as to what the price of wheat will be three months ahead is headed for disaster. It is easy to come into this house now and say how sure we were six months ago of what was going to happen in the wheat markets of the world to-day. I wonder whether the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar would not help those of us who have an interest in wheat by telling us what the market is going to be three months hence. If he and the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-[DOT] who, I think, has some claim to knowledge with respect to the marketing of wheat, because he has been engaged in it as a farmer and to some extent as a merchant over a long period of years-were so wise last fall, will they not be good enough to tell us poor ignoramuses now what the price of wheat is going to be three months hence, six months hence? Is it going up or is it going down?
Mr. Speaker, will the minister permit me-?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Why, surely. If I can get an answer to that question, it will mean a lot.
If the evidence now were as plain that the price is going up as it was in July last that it was going up, I should be glad to give the minister the advice at once.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Surely that is begging the question.
Not so far off.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is a continuous problem.
So was that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Along the line of the argument advanced by my hon. friend-if his line of policy is to be followed-someone will have to predict what is going to be done three months hence. It is not sufficient merely to take action when the evidence is plain. You are not in this business for one day or one week. What faced the government of Canada last fall was that it was in the wheat business to a greater extent than any other organization in the world had ever been. Joseph in Egypt was a piker compared with the government of Canada. We

Wheat Board-Mr. Dunning
had a very great volume of wheat, and who owned it? The people of Canada. They had taken delivery of it. They had paid a price for it, a price which was greater than the price which up to that time they had been able to obtain in the markets of the world when they went to sell it. The people of Canada were holding the bag for the farmers of western Canada. I am not quarrelling with the policy in that regard. In a national crisis such as was involved in relation to the wheat business it was necessary for this nation to take some action with regard to a national asset of such tremendous importance. But the people owned that wheat-nearly 300,000,000 bushels of it, as the hon. member for Qu'Appelle indicated. There are two peculiar things about wheat. One is that wheat is ripening somewhere in the world all the time. The second is that the wheat that you did not eat last year you cannot, increasing your consumption, eat this year. With respect to some commodities a decrease in consumption during a period is followed' by increased consumptive demand at some later period. It is not true of wheat. That people were deprived of wheat or did not eat it a year ago does not mean that they will eat twice or one and a half times as much this year. These are two important facts to bear in mind in connection with wheat.
The government had this enormous liability. It had another problem-which brings me to my second point. Another crop was coming along in western Canada, a crop which at that time and until its disposal was owned by the individual fanner producing it. It was in the highest national interest that the individual farmer who owned the growing crop of 1936 should be put in a position to get the best possible price for it. Who was the greatest competitor with that growing crop? The government of Canada, owning the vast quantity of wheat to which I have made reference. In the light of those circumstances what was the best policy to follow? To make provision for further increasing the load of wheat carried by the government, or so to handle that load as to give the farmers of western Canada the maximum possible opportunity of disposing of their new crop? The course the government took involved two or three major advantages of a national character, and some considerable advantages to the farmers of western Canada. I will deal with the latter first.
What was the advantage to the farmer of western Canada? First, the announcement of the government policy rendered utterly impossible bear raiding during the process of

rush marketing. There was no possibility ol organized bear speculation forcing down the price of wheat for the farmer's new crop. Why? Because the world had notice that the government of Canada was prepared to take delivery at any time the price was forced down to ninety cents. That was a degree of protection which the farmers of western Canada have never enjoyed during all the period of their marketing-never in the world. In consequence, for the first time during a period of free marketing, there was no attempt at a bear raid during the time of rush marketing of the 1936 crop. That was one advantage reaped by the farmers of western Canada. As the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) reminds me, the development of bear raiding was already apparent before we took action. It was plain to be seen.
What was the second point? The greatest competitor of the farmer of western Canada in the marketing of his 1936 crop was the wheat board holding these hundreds of millions of bushels of old wheat. Always in the past the size of the carry-over from the preceding crop has had a bearish price influence upon the new crop-always. The larger the carryover of old wheat the more likelihood is there of successful bear raids on the price of new wheat. What happened? By the development of the government's policy, for the first time in the history of open market wheat trading, there was from the farmer's point of view no carry-over in competition with the marketing of his new wheat. Why was that? It was because the wheat board did not sell any old wheat in competition with the rush marketing by the farmer of wheat of the new crop. The government continued to hold back, as it had been holding back for years; it kept out of the farmer's way and left him a free rein to sell his 1936 crop without the bearish influence of any carry-over from the old year.
That, I believe, was a major service rendered by the people of all Canada to the people of western Canada, and the only reason that there is criticism to-day is that the gentlemen who are criticizing now have the advantage of hindsight, which, of course, in argument is converted into foresight. The price of wheat has gone up. It has gone up very largely because of the steady, persistent selling policy adopted as a result of this government's wheat policy. It has gone up largely by reason-
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I should like to answer
the question but I cannot hear it.

Wheat Board-Mr. Dunning

What put the price
down?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) gave us several very sound reasons why the price went down in previous years, but I do not intend to be diverted from 1936 into previous years. I am discussing the amendment now before the house, which relates to the government's policy with respect to the marketing of wheat in 1936 as set forth in the order in council. In addition, we performed, by reason of this policy, a further great service to the farmers of western Canada, and without injuring the national well-being in so doing. The hon. member for Rosthern touched on it. For the first time in the history of marketing in western Canada cooperative marketing on the pool plan was made possible, insured against any loss on the part of the pools. Think what that means. We are all aware of the great disaster which overtook the pool marketing organizations in consequence of having made during one year a larger initial payment than they were afterwards able to realize from the wheat. We know that the provinces concerned, which undertook a part of the load resulting from that occurrence, became financially embarrassed. We know that subsequently the former government of Canada had to come to the rescue, and we know that because of that the tremendous load of wheat developed.
Now in 1936 for the first time the wheat pool could have said to all farmers, "Deliver your wheat to the pool; you will get 87i cents as an initial payment and whatever else we may make out of the wheat as a result of its disposal in due course." I am not criticizing the pools for not taking that step; that is their business. Nor am I foolish enough to overlook the fact that they are one of the greatest business organizations in Canada, one of the most powerful in point of size of assets and control of volume of commodity-because it has been said repeatedly that the wheat pools control normally forty-seven per cent of the wheat. See what an opportunity was given by the government of Canada to the cooperative organization controlling forty-seven per cent of the wheat to operate a pool and make an initial payment without any fear of loss in so doing, because the government would come in and take delivery of the wheat at 871 cents. Why that was not done remains a matter of policy with the pools themselves; they had a perfect right to make a decision. But I have a perfect right to point out that the policy of the government would have enabled the wheat
pools to give to all of their customers all of the advantage, if any, which has come about by the increased price of wheat since that time and without any risk of loss to the pools, for the first time in the history of cooperative marketing in the west.

When was
that offer made to the pools on the part of the government?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No offer was made; the order in council itself constituted the offer.
What was the date of it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
August 28, I believe. But it does not matter what the date was, the effect is just the same. Prior to that date every farmer marketing his wheat had a right to market with the board at 87J cents initial payment. The extent to which he did so prior to that date was indicated by the Minister of Agriculture. There were 38,000,000 marketed and 600,000 delivered to the wheat board. Those figures constitute in my opinion the main reason why the pool organization decided not to continue, not to go ahead as a pooling organization on the same basis. I am not questioning their wisdom; that is an internal matter for themselves; but I do point out that they are very powerful organizations. If anything in Canada can be described as a truly big interest, then the western cooperative marketing organization engaged in the marketing of wheat can truly be described as a big interest-and I am not using that term in any critical or disrespectful sense. The wheat pools, with their expert knowledge gained by experience in this business, aided as they might have been by the advance knowledge of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar and the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, have some responsibilities. The government of Canada have many other responsibilities besides wheat. The cooperative organizations are organized specifically to deal with this problem, and when the government of Canada by order in council under the wheat board act, lays down a policy saying to these organizations: "Go out and market your wheat cooperatively; make an initial payment of 87i cents a bushel, being insured against loss by the fact that the government of Canada will take delivery at that figure," it seems to me that the people of Canada are supporting in a very fair way the cooperative marketing of wheat in western Canada.
I think there is nothing further I wish to say, except that, as one who believes in cooperative marketing and not state socialism,



Wheat Board,-Mr. Dunning
I believe that the government of Canada on behalf of the people of Canada should extend to wheat growers or anyone else the maximum assistance in the way of promoting self-help on the part of those directly interested. I believe that the order in council of last August was truly cooperative in the spirit of what I have just said. It represented a degree of cooperation on the part of the people of the whole of Canada with those who are joined together in an effort to market a commodity, and I doubt very much if we whose hearts are in the life of western Canada shall make any progress by attempting to follow the line of state socialism, by attempting to dragoon the whole of Canada into applying the principles of state socialism to the marketing of our chief product; because quite obviously if we insist on support for that we must be content to move in the direction of state socialism in the marketing of many other commodities as well as wheat. I believe that governmental assistance in the marketing of all these commodities can best be given by helping those who are engaged in the cooperative marketing of their own products to help themselves.

I am one of those who rather appreciate the amendment moved by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley). I say so for this reason-and I offer this as a criticism of the government: I do not think the story of the reasons for the action that was taken last fall with respect to wheat board legislation was sufficiently told. The debate on this amendment will do a good deal towards clarifying the situation with regard to the action taken when the government declared its wheat board policy of last year. This I think will be appreciated not only by hon. members of this house but by all who are particularly interested in the problem as far as western Canada is concerned.
I think it will be readily apparent now, '.f it was not before, that there is a wide diversity of opinion, not only in western Canada but throughout the whole dominion, as to the best policy for marketing wheat. During the past twenty odd years we have had in reality three different marketing systems. First we had the war-time wheat board, which was really set up for the purpose of keeping the price of wheat down. I think the opportunities and accomplishments of that board, under circumstances which were unique, have led a good many people to think that the same things can be done by a wheat board under very different circumstances. Many people to-day having those results in mind, think of another wheat board as being able to accomplish similar results.

Following that wheat board we had the voluntary pool. When the government of Canada and the provincial governments failed to implement the legislation creating the wheat board, farmer organizations in the three western provinces set about establishing a voluntary wheat pool. In that they were reasonably successful. It was followed a few years later by an attempt to create a one hundred per cent pool owned and controlled by the farmers' organizations. That attempt was not successful. Then we have had the open market system, sometimes called the speculative market, in which the grain is moved into the different positions by open market trading. May I digress for a moment with respect to the so-called speculative marketing of wheat? I cannot for the life of me see how we can get away from it. When you look at the market page of any newspaper you find quotations for products throughout the world, reflected in markets in different places. They have to come to some point where a price is established. Even last year when the crop which is at present being marketed was in its growing season Mr. McFarland made a forecast as to what in his judgment that crop would amount to. I am not going to argue whether his judgment was right or wrong, but in that sense he speculated as to the prospects of the crop. Unfortunately he was in error.
Crop prospects throughout the world, particularly with respect to wheat, have a definite effect on the prevailing price. When the different markets of the world have an opportunity of forming a judgment with respect to the conditions and requirements of the world these judgments converge in some quarter, and the recognized place is the Liverpool market. We have had argument as to whether a wheat board under government control, or the pool, farmer-owned and farmer-controlled if you like, is the more desirable to establish in this country. As far as I am concerned I subscribe to the policy of the farmers owning and controlling their own marketing organization, and I think our western Canadian farmers have an opportunity to establish for themselves a very creditable marketing organization. The only difference I see is that probably a government wheat board backed by the resources of the state might be stronger financially than would the farmers with their own resources alone. But in that regard there is the possibility that the government could assist to some extent a cooperative grain marketing organization.
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle undoubtedly had something in view in moving this amendment, and no doubt it was that the

Wheat Board-Mr. Weir
prices of wheat andi other grains have improved considerably since the beginning of the crop season. I am wondering where my hon. friend and those associated1 with him, particularly the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), were in 1932. Were they shedding the same crocodile tears at that time when the price was ranging in the neighbourhood of 30 cents a bushel? That is when something should have been said by way of protest, and an attempt made to establish a reasonable price. Here I wish to make a further observation with respect to government policy at that time. The government in its wisdom decided to adopt the policy of sound money, and I agree with the argument of previous speakers this afternoon that that policy had a decided influence on the prices received for the primary products of this country, particularly those sold on the English market.
I think all of us are inclined to reflect the opinions expressed in our home districts and communities, and give a good deal of thought to the observations that come to us from time to time. I am one of those who were obliged to attend one of the so-calledl pool protest meetings last year. But before I touch on that I should like to make one other observation. No doubt the policy of a government where a democracy is working properly should reflect in legislation what are the desires and wishes of the people. I do not mean that as supposed leaders of public thought we should not use every possible opportunity to guide that thought; but when we go home we listen to the observations and representations made by various individuals and organizations with respect to different questions. In regard to the marketing of wheat we find perhaps as many differences of opinion throughout the length and breadth of this country as there are upon any other question.
As I said a moment ago, I attended one of these wheat pool protest meetings, and this afternoon I intend to take here exactly the same position I took there.
_ May I go back just one step? This meeting I suppose was similar to those attended by other hon. gentlemen, protesting against the government's action in passing the order in council which prohibited the wheat boards accepting wheat unless the price dropped below 90 cents per bushel. But may I tell you, Mr. Speaker, that in 1930, a few days after I accepted the nomination as candidate for the constituency of Macdonald, and when the wheat pool was probably at the height of its power, I attended a meeting in my
home town attended by some four or five hundred people who were there to protest against the payments that the pool were making and to protest also against being tied to their contracts and forced to deliver further wheat to the pool organization.
In my district, as in other districts, opportunity was afforded to the growers to organize a one hundred per cent pool. That proposal was turned down. An attempt was made to establish a poultry marketing organization in western Canada, and it will be remembered that these same people turned that down very decidedly. So I think you will agree, Mr. Speaker, that sometimes because of the many divergencies of opinion it is very difficult to know exactly what is in the minds of people who are carrying on an agitation to promote certain marketing policies or, as a matter of fact, policies of any kind. Sometimes it is impossible to get enough of these people to put their names on the dotted line to bring about the desired result.
With regard to last year's crop, undoubtedly the early prospects were reasonably good. That mu9t have been recognized by those who travelled through the west, particularly through the northern sections of Manitoba. Even Mr. McFarland, who is undoubtedly a man of considerable experience in the grain business, realized that fact. The observations I am about to make have been made before, but perhaps it will do no harm to repeat them. The government made no change in the marketing policy of the board during the first twenty-seven days of this marketing season; in other words the board was free to accept wheat at the initial payment of 87^ cents a bushel. During that period, with a guaranteed price of 87J cents and an opportunity provided to deliver to the board and to participate in any increased price, the board received only one and a half per cent of the deliveries made.
Going a step further and referring to the crop of 1935-36, when the price of wheat was above the board's price only forty-seven per cent of the elevator deliveries were sold to the board; but when the price fell below the board's price sales to the board increased to one hundred and forty per cent of the deliveries to the elevators. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that when a board is so uncertain what its deliveries and what its opportunities for selling that wheat will be, its opportunity to accomplish results that might be comparable with those obtained through open market operations or otherwise, is certainly very limited.
I have not been in this house very long Mr. Speaker, I admit, but I have been here long enough to learn to recognize the realities
i906
Wheat Board-Mr. Weir

of a situation. Hon. members opposite, particularly my hon. friend from Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) and my hon. friend from Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), if they realize anything at all must appreciate that there is a very decided difference of opinion on the question of the government's being in the grain business at all. Undoubtedly that difference of opinion is reflected in this house, as well as throughout the entire dominion. What I wish to point out to my hon. friends, the reality which I should like them to face, is this: Even supposing it was possible to secure the support of every member from the four western provinces for a government wheat board, you would have only seventy-one members out of a house of two hundred and forty-five members. To me that is the practical side of the situation. I do not say that you would be able to get the support of every western member for such a proposal, but even if you could get all the members from the four western provinces to support a measure providing for the marketing of wheat through a government board you would have only the number I have indicated. That to me is the crux of the situation, and I can quite appreciate the position in which the government found themselves last fall when they attempted to deal with this matter.
