If we are to adopt a policy of state assistance in the marketing of wheat I should like to ask my hon. friend who proposed this amendment how we can refuse the same assistance in the marketing of fish, live stock, lumber and other primary products that are sold on the markets of the world. So I say that if we are going to give assistance in the marketing of wheat we should consider all the factors involved, and particularly what the consequences may be in connection with the marketing of other commodities. Many hon. members of this house from eastern Canada have protested strongly against the prices being received for fish, dairy products and other commodities, and they have said very unkind things to me at least, and I am sure to other hon. gentlemen, with respect to the action of the government in regard to wheat.
There is another point that I think is of sufficient importance to be referred to at this time. Since 1930 this country has been accumulating large surpluses of wheat. At the same time we were coaxing and begging European countries to purchase additional quantities of Canadian wheat. Many protests have come to the government against their action in interfering, as the buyers claimed, with the normal flow of wheat; in other words, the buyers did not think they

were being given the chance to buy Canadian wheat at a price that had any relation to open market competition. This year, when the condition is completely reversed and there is a possibility of greatly increased prices, I think that having in mind the desirability of selling our wheat in the export market, the government of necessity must take notice of that sentiment that exists abroad. They are in a very much better position to say to the European buyer, who, after all, is the most important factor in our established price structure, that with prices increasing the government has nothing whatever to do with the situation, and that they are buying their wheat in open competition on the same basis as all other buyers.
I believe we cannot emphasize too strongly the fact that Canada must maintain the goodwill of those who are purchasing wheat. Any action, particularly on the part of the government, which would in any way cause ill feeling and react to the detriment of this country, or any action by the government to maintain prices higher than they should be, would be a dangerous policy for us to follow.
Some hon. members have gone so far in their accusations as to say that the present chairman of the wheat board was a grain exchange man. It has been my privilege to know Mr. Murray for a considerable time. I believe I do not overstate it when I say that he was one of the men who many years ago recognized the possibility of pool marketing methods. He was one of the men who promoted in its early stages the pool idea among farmer organizations. He was one of those who helped to draft the first contract and, as I recall it, even went so far as to prepare the agreement used in the initial stages by the pools in their dealings with the elevator companies, whereby the elevator companies would handle pool grain on the specific basis set out in that agreement. For these reasons I submit that the reflections on Mr. Murray's ability and character have not been to the good; certainly they have not been fair to him. I suggest, on the other hand, that the house must recognize that Mr. Murray has done a good job in marketing wheat. Through his operations he has relieved the market of the surplus standing over, one which undoubtedly would have had a bad effect on the price for this year's crop.
When he took over in his official capacity the board held 298,000,000 bushels of wheat. He received a further 48,000,000 bushels, which meant that he had to handle over 346,000,000 bushels. That being so, and with a crop to be marketed, if he could get into a position

Wheat Board-Mr. Weir
where the carryover or surplus at the end of this crop year was down to reasonable proportions, a good deal of the credit must be due to his activities.
Many hon. members have criticized the actions of the government, and have suggested that it could have foretold what the price trend was going to be for this season's crop. May I place this observation before them: Even as late as the end of June Mr. McFarland made a forecast. At that time the size of our crop was by no means known-at least not definitely. Of course it was known that the United States crop had been somewhat damaged. May I point out, as was done this afternoon by the Minister of Finance, that we cannot limit our operations to a month-to-month policy or, if you like, to a three-month policy. There has to be a long range view taken of the situation. Had there been a normal crop in the United States last year, and a reasonable crop in Canada, one can readily appreciate the different circumstances that would have existed.
Through the board, I believe the government has recognized the position of the wheat farmers. We must give them credit for their action in at least this one respect, that they refrained from selling while the delivery season was at its height, thus leaving the market wide open for the farmers and giving them an opportunity to sell without government wheat board competition and as well with a guaranteed price of 87i cents per bushel. One cannot help smiling at the reflections made by hon. gentlemen opposite and at their claims that everybody could have been sure that the price of wheat was going to go up. I had no such assurance personally, and I gave no advice. But with the sure knowledge these hon. gentlemen now claim to have had, certainly they could have made good fellows of themselves if they had gone out and urged their friends to hold their wheat, and buy futures. That might have been a good way of definitely guaranteeing re-election. However, if the price had gone the other way the results might not have been so good.
Turning to the amendment of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) I note that he was careful to draft it in a cute manner. It is in these words:
This house regrets that the government rendered the Canadian Wheat Board Act, 1935, inoperative in its application to the 1936 *wheat crop.
In other words, he has attempted to limit the discussion to that particular phase of the question. He knows it is a want of confidence
motion, and that those who support it declare themselves to be totally lacking in confidence in the policies of the government. May I say to him that I, too, regretted the action which the government took last year. I thought they had made a mistake. At the same time I am not prepared to say that to date all the government's policies have been wrong. His proposal is undoubtedly designed to place western members on the spot. In confining his amendment to one specific question he is attempting to limit discussion to that one phase of government policy.
I shall not attempt to say anything on the constitutional issue raised by the right hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett). I believe his observations were effectively met this afternoon by the hon. member for Rosthem (Mr. Tucker). His explanation has been the clearest that has been given so far, and I, for one, am grateful for the contribution he has made.
As I have said, I regretted the action of the board at the time, but I must say that I am grateful to the hon. member for Qu'Appelle for moving the amendment, for by so doing he has forced, if you like, or has obliged, if you care to use that word, some ministers and some hon. members to come forward and tell their stories.
They have not told it all, though.

I say again I had hoped that the wheat board would operate, but the difficulty which presented itself in connection with establishing a price was one of the important factors which had to be taken into account. It is all very well for some hon. members to argue that a price should have been set sufficiently high to ensure that a considerable quantity of grain would be delivered to the board. May I say in that regard that if I understand anything about the marketing of grain and the establishing of a price, it would be necessary to do it at the beginning of a crop year. No one can deny that an initial payment of 87i cents per bushel at the beginning of last year's season would have been considered a reasonable price at that time. I do not believe even the wheat pools, had they been functioning as formerly, would have set a higher initial payment. I doubt if many people in Canada were disposed seriously to urge the government to set a higher price at a point higher than 874 cents per bushel, having regard to the future and the possibility of the state being obliged to make contributions if there were losses.
Wheat Board-Mr. Weir

I regret the action which the government took at that time. I think they made a political blunder so far as western Canada is concerned. At the time I thought it was an error, but I recognized the facts of the situation. I say to the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) who moved this amendment that the majority of the people in this country are not very sympathetic toward the government being in the grain business. That being so, all the strength that hon. members opposite can muster will not be sufficient. When the government of Canada goes into the wheat marketing business, it has to take into consideration the viewpoints of different parts of the country. If western Canada can claim the support of only 71 members out of 245, there is a situation which ought to be faced.
I am one of those who appreciate what the hon. member (Mr. Perley) has done. He knows perfectly well that his amendment is a want of confidence motion. Had he not made it a want of confidence motion as applied to the entire policy of the government I should have been inclined to support him. I would not trade the wheat marketing policy of this government for the wheat marketing policy of its predecessors in office.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to place a few words on record in regard to the stand I took in my own riding with reference to the continuation of the Canadian wheat board. The amendment before the house reads:
This house regrets that the government rendered the Canadian Wheat Board Act, 1935, inoperative in its application to the 1936 wheat crop.
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) who moved that amendment put the word "regrets" in it, but I doubt very much whether his regrets are as substantial as he would like to make them appear.

Speak for
yourself.

I'm doing that. It has been said that some men are born great, that others aspire to greatness while others have greatness thrust upon them. I should like to parody these statements and say that some men are born destructive, others aspire to destruction while others have the methods and policies of destruction thrust upon them. As I read this amendment, it is purely destructive. I think the one outstanding idea in the back of the head of the hon. member who moved the amendment was to divide the western members of this house on this wheat board

issue-divide and destroy. The hon. member is actually attempting to destroy the influence of the Liberal party in western Canada. His desire to put me on the spot does not make a bit of difference to me. I rather like to think that a member of the Conservative party thinks he can put me on the spot, and then gives me an opportunity to prove that he cannot.
I have no hesitation in saying that this amendment is a motion of want of confidence in everything the government has done since it came into office and in every policy and principle sponsored and accepted by the Liberal party. I feel sure that when this amendment is put to a vote it will not command any support worth speaking of on this side of the house.
Or on this side.

There is no doubt that the vote will be overwhelmingly against the motion.
I was surprised the other day to hear the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) say that he opposed the policy of this government on the wheat board and supported this want of confidence motion. He argued that what had been done was unconstitutional and illegal. That does not come with very good grace from the leader of the party which opposed a report brought down in 1928 and again in 1929 by the industrial and international relations committee dealing with a matter of great social importance; that is, insurance against unemployment, sickness and invalidity. The view of the committee was that they should take the advice of the law officers of the crown in drawing up their report, and their final report was that this measure could be worked out only by following along the orbit of provincial jurisdiction. Hon. members of the Conservative party got up in this house and staged a debate opposing the report of the committee. They said the report was not sound, that the jurisdiction rested with the federal parliament.
But they did not stop at that. When they were in power between 1930 and 1935 they enacted legislation which in effect announced to the country that the federal jurisdiction was sufficient. Their position in this respect has been rendered untenable by the decision of the privy council, which has recently declared this legislation to be ultra vires. We are now back to where we were in 1928 and 1929. Eight or nine years have been thus wasted in inaugurating necessary

Wheat Board-Mr. McIntosh
social legislation, and I place the responsibility where it in a great degree belongs-on the present opposition in this House of Commons.
When that was their stand a few years ago in connection with social legislation of outstanding national importance, what must we say to them to-day when they tell us that the stand taken by this government on the wheat board is unconstitutional? Since the Conservative party and its leader were wrong before, I d>o not think we can go far astray if we conclude that they are wrong again. The stand which this government has taken is legal and constitutional-not illegal and unconstitutional as hon. members say. We have the opinion of the law officers of the crown, and not to follow out that opinion is only an excuse for delay and inactivity. It is said that for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. There has been no equal and opposite reaction in a judicial way, in a constitutional way or in a legal way to the action taken by the government. That being the case up to the present time, I think I am on sound ground when I say that there is not much to the argument of the leader of the opposition that the stand of the government was unconstitutional. Yesterday the hon.* member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) in discussing this question, made a few statements to which I should like to draw attention. He said:
We are, and we always have been, in competition with the world.
I think he is correct in that statement. I do not think there is any doubt but that the world is the ultimate economic and industrial reality and that a country which does not fit its policies into the world as a whole will certainly not go very far in the race, nationally or internationally. The same applies to a party. If-and this statement cannot be challenged-the world in an economic and an industrial sense is ultimately a single reality, then to be effective a party's policies must be in accord as far as possible with that world entity or reality. To the degree in which that principle is carried out the policies of any party will be efficient and successful. I believe the Liberal party has always tried to recognize that objective, that its outlook is for world trade linked with national business established on a sound and progressive basis.
A little later the hon. member said:
Other nations are protecting their industries by means of tariffs, quotas, subsidies, marketing boards and the like. All this is largely a development of the last twenty years.
So far as Canada is concerned, it has not been a development of the last twenty years. Our protective policies have been a development of the years since 1878. When in that year the people pronounced upon economic policies they pronounced in favour of high protection, and they have had just what they asked for, ever since that time. We talk a lot about freer trade and free trade. Yet even in 1930, when in western Canada the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) courageously told the people that if he were returned to power he would raise protection to a high level, thousands upon thousands of votes in every constituency in Saskatchewan and throughout the west were cast in support of that policy-which would almost lead me to the conclusion that if we are to have progressive trade policies the people themselves will have to take a more determined stand. As I have pointed out, protectionism has been a development not merely of the past twenty years but of the much longer period since confederation.
The hon. member for Lethbridge comes practically to the conclusion that since we have high protection in Canada-the Liberal party is trying to pare it down, but it is more easily raised than reduced-we should accept the other alternative of setting to work to nationalize the marketing of every primary product and adopting a system of state socialism. As far as I am concerned I could not accept a policy of that kind. Neither can the Liberal party.
Mr. Speaker, I never said at any time that we should have state socialism, nor have I advocated any such thing. The hon. member is giving his own conclusions, not mine.
I am very happy to hear that, and I accept the hon. member's explanation. It was high tariffs instead.
It is not an explanation; it is a straight denial.

All right. The hon. member went on to state that we had a price spreads inquiry from which, he inferred, practically no results flowed. I would draw his attention to the fact that, outside of the publicity which the inquiry gave to social and industrial conditions in Canada, it resulted in the passing of the Trade and Industry Commission Act, which was declared intra vires by the privy council.
Only in part.

Well, if only in part,
it would go to show that the investigation was along the right lines, and that we might
Wheat Board-Mr. McIntosh

well add to that power of investigation and regulation, as we are doing in amending the Combines Investigation Act.
The hon. member further says:
Canada has all too recklessly left her primary producers to look after themselves.
Is not self-preservation the first law of nature? My own opinion is that when it comes down to a vote on fiscal, industrial and financial policies, if the primary producers go wrong and vote for a protective policy, what can you do for them? Nothing. It is hard to assist a class of people who say one thing to-day and perhaps the opposite to-morrow.
Vote for a free trade government !

You mean freer trade.
The primary producers of this country must take a definite stand against high protection, and not do what has been done too often before in the last seventy years. They must nail their colours to the mast and say that they want more free trade, more exchange of commodities, and a policy in harmony with the fact that after all the world is the final economic entity that must be reckoned with.
I now pass on for a few moments to some statements made by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). At page 1879 of Hansard he stated that-
Liberal candidates in Saskatchewan did tell the producers of w-estern Canada that the wheat hoard system of marketing would not be endangered by the return of a Liberal government. That, I believe, all members of this house from western Canada will recollect.
As one member, I do not recollect it because I did not say it. I put my confidence in the Liberal party, its leaders and the people. I was satisfied that if the people returned the Liberal party to power without it having made too many promises or indefinite statements, the right type of policy, financial and industrial, would be inaugurated and a new era for the industrialist, the producer and consumer would result.
The hon. member made another statement which I should like to contradict. He said:
... I stated over and over again that in my opinion steps should be taken by any government elected to open up the channels of trade, and that any steps taken in the opposite direction would have dire results upon our political economy.
I have always understood that the group to which the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar belongs is opposed to free and freer trade. They believe in policies of self-sufficiency, of narrow nationalism and state socialism, and they are absolutely opposed to international trade. I had to meet that issue

in my own riding in 1935; I demolished those who took the opposite viewpoint, and I am ready to do it again.
Will the hon. member give his authority for stating that the group to which we belong is opposed to international trade? That is, will he quote the statement from our platform?

It is not necessary. It
is plastered all over your platform and characteristic of all your public utterances.
Over what?

He is trying to
plaster it now.

It is not necessary-the job is complete. I want to hurry on. I am astonished at the temerity of the hon. member in coming into this house and making assertions of that kind, when every member of his incoherent group, himself included, made statements of policy of a direct opposite nature. Further, the hon. member says:
To my mind the preelection speeches of some at least of our prominent Liberal membere u'ere interpreted as promising a fire sale policy for Canadian wheat should a Liberal government be returned to power.
There was no suggestion whatever of anything in the nature of a fire sale of wheat so far as the North Battleford constituency was concerned'. The people of that constituency knew precisely what legislation had been enacted and1 they inferred that the legislation setting up a wheat board meant that the board would continue. But as to any suggestion of a fire sale policy, I say emphatically that no such thing was discussed in my riding. There was nothing of that kind suggested in connection with the sale of wheat, and therefore this statement of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar is at variance with the facts.
As regards your constituency.
That applies to the whole of western Canada.
You cannot speak for all western Canada.

I can speak as well as you can and perhaps a little better. The hon. gentleman makes this further statement:
To-day hon. members from western Canada sitting on the opposite side of the house have an opportunity of registering in this house the protests they made last August and September.
There is not very much in an argument of that kind. There is absolutely no reason why a member of parliament may not take a

Wheat Board-Mr. McIntosh
definite stand on any matter of government policy in his own riding without regarding it as incumbent upon him to come to Ottawa and re-hash the whole thing over again. I say, Mr. Speaker, there is no gumption in an argument of that kind ; and if the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) tries to put me on the spot in that regard he is simply wasting his breath because I am delighted to stand here and answer him in his own coin. But if it comes to a question of any member's attitude on matters of policy, I can go back a little in history and tell the house what my stand has been on some important matters. I do not know where the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar stood in 1917 on one particular question, but I can assure him that at that time I opposed the iniquitous War-Time Elections Act. I opposed' national conscription, and was practically alone in my opposition to it in Saskatchewan. As a newspaperman I stood alone.
Are you proud of it?

Yes, I am; conscription was not necessary. Again, when the party opposite put through the gerrymander in Saskatchewan in 1933 I was the first member to go home and tell my people what had been done, and took a definite stand in my own riding in opposition to such a policy. With regard to the action of the government last summer, I should like to tell the house exactly what my position was at that particular time. When the government made its decision my own opinion was that they had made a great mistake, though I admit that the opposite view may, in time turn out to be a short range view and that from a long range point of view the decision of the government may' prove to be the correct one. At any rate when the government made their decision- and they had a perfect right to decide the matter, for the people sent them here for that purpose-as the member for the North. Battle-ford constituency I took the stand that as an emergency measure the wheat board should have been allowed to function for another year. I took the view that it should function as an emergency board, not as a permanent institution. Before the government made their decision there came to my office in North Battleford a telegram from the pool organization at Regina, as follows:
Regina, Sask,
Aug. 20, 1936.
C. R. McIntosh, M.P.
North Battleford, Sask.
Press dispatches in Leader Post this morning state that federal government has decided to allow minimum wheat price paid by wheat board to remain at 87i cents basis one Northern
Fort William according to report from well informed quarters. Dispatch ends quote Western Liberal members appear to be satisfied with the continuation of the old minimum price unquote. Our organization vitally interested amount initial payment and believe that should be set in relation to production cost which is substantially higher than amount indicated. Our board would appreciate your reaction on this statement.
Sask. Co-Op. Wheat Producers Ltd.
I have been in business in North Battleford for twenty-five years, and altogether apart from politics I have always supported the pool. As a public man, though not as a politician, I stood by them, and throughout that period of twenty-five years I have come in contact with the leading grain growers of the province as well as the leading officials of the pool. Our relations have been quite friendly and indeed we have been co-partners in the upbuilding of the province. So that the stand I took on this occasion was nothing new; in fact, I could not follow any other course and be consistent with my past action. If I had done anything else it would have been opposing the pool to no good purpose, and therefore when this telegram came I wired back-
What are you quoting from?

I am quoting from a copy of my own newspaper, the North Battleford News; of course it cannot be contradicted. The telegram I sent in reply reads:
North Battleford, Sask.
August 20, 1936.
Sask. Co-Op. Wheat Producers Ltd.
Regina, Sask.
Wire fixed minimum wheat price received. Nothing final heard regarding decision federal government fix minimum price 874 cents bushel. Am Western Liberal member and represent large farming population but do not "appear" nor am I satisfied with continuation old minimum price. Agree with your organization fixed minimum price should be higher and that an initial payment certainly should be set, possessing fair and definite relationship with cost of production. Production costs higher in north. Take stand fixed minimum should run from dollar ten to dollar fifteen cents bushel thus assuring farmers satisfactory initial payment.
Cameron McIntosh.
That was one step I took; I should like to put another on record. After that telegram had been dispatched, the decision of the government being far from satisfactory, a large mass meeting was held in North Battleford. It was quite spontaneous, for I saw no large bills advertising the meeting; the only bills I came across were very small ones of the dodger size.	[DOT]

Printed in your office?
Wheat Board-Mr. McIntosh

No, in my opponent's office. About four hundred persons, farmers and business men, attended the meeting, and the chairman was Mr. W. A. Campbell, manager of the Western Groceries.
It is only fair to say that that audience was made up of Liberals, Conservatives and those who supported policies of socialism and other isms of that kind. After the matter was discussed the meeting decided to put a resolution before the gathering and have it accepted. That resolution was unanimously, passed, handed to me and I wired it as quickly as possible to Hon. J. G. Gardiner, the Minister of Agriculture, coupling with it the following words:
Public meeting farmers and business men held here Saturday strongly protested government's announced wheat policy tantamount destruction wheat board because of failure to establish fixed minimum price guaranteeing cost production plus fair profit. Preferred treatment manufacturers compared with shabby consideration given agriculturists has aroused much resentment and bitter opposition. Personally consider government emergency policy far from satisfactory and would therefore respectfully urge immediate and serious consideration same.
Then the resolution follows:
Resolution unanimously endorsed by gathering approximately four hundred as follows:
"This meeting protests the action of the dominion government in discontinuing operation of the wheat board by leaving a stop loss price of 87 j cent per bushel basis No. 1 northern Fort William and prohibiting delivery to the board unless market closes at 90 cents per bushel or less.
"Therefore be it resolved that this meeting demand the federal government authorize wheat board to announce immediately a minimum price of $1.15 basis 1 northern Fort William, and further that this wheat board establish its own sales agencies with a view to marketing wheat direct to final purchasers, and further that this meeting requests C. R. McIntosh, M.P. to present this resolution and opinions expressed at this meeting to the government, using his influence to have same accepted by the government.
That was signed by myself.
That was the stand I took in my own constituency on that question. And my stand in that regard was nothing new, nothing strange. I have already said that for the twenty-four years preceding that date I had always done my best to support the pool when it could be done, not that I accepted their policies a hundred per cent but because as a business organization backed by the farmers it was desirable to give them support and strengthen their hands in the solution of the many problems confronting them.

Would the
hon. member mind putting on record the answer he received to that wire?

I have not the answer here, but it was that the government would give the matter its consideration, as asked by the meeting. I take it for granted that that is all that could be expected as an immediate answer to any such wire.
Before and after that meeting resolutions came in from all over the riding. I shall just mention a few that came, I shall not read them. They came from wheat pool committees at Maymont; Ruddell; Radisson; R.R. 2, North Battleford; Hafford; Brada; Redfield; K eat ley; Krydor; Mullinger; Paradise Hill; Struan; Rabbit Lake; Belbutte; Bapaume; Bolney; Hatherleigh; St. Walburg; Cleeves; Whitkow; Medstead and Langham, and from the Radisson town council, the North Battleford board of trade, Rural Municipality No. 407 Round Hill, a public meeting in the town of Radisson, North Battleford rural municipality No. 437, Spiritwood rural municipality, Hamlin district farmers, Maymont district farmers, Borden district farmers, a mass meeting of Krydor farmers and Douglas rural municipality.
These are practically all the resolutions I received on the decision of the government. After the mass meeting in North Battleford and after the stand I took in my constituency, and after these resolutions were received, the farmers in the riding took it for granted that all was done that could be done, and since that time I have heard of very little opposition in that constituency. Everything done was done above-board, was reported in the press, and my own stand as a member was given to the people in such a way that I do not think there was much doubt as to where I stood in the entire matter.
In closing, you may ask what is to be my stand on the amendment before the house? It can be readily understood from what I have said. My stand will be to oppose the want of confidence resolution and to support the Prime Minister of this country and every member of the cabinet, and especially the Minister of Agriculture in his arduous duties, and to uphold the policy of the Liberal party as a policy which in the long run and even now must work out beneficially to the whole nation. The improvement in exports and imports, the prosperity which is evident on all sides, and the new encouragement that is being given to the people everywhere is 1 think complete proof that the trade and agricultural policies of the government are in

Wheat Board-Division
line with its traditional policy of freer trade, getting into all the markets of the world and thereby giving the rank and file of this country purchasing power which is sure to bring
prosperity.

I was paired with the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Gray). Had I voted I would have voted in favour of the amendment.
Motion (Mr. Dunning) agreed to and the house went into committee of ways and means, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is difficult to generalize, and it is particularly difficult to give a comparison of the rates affecting the different items. Since 1930 there have been between 400 and 500 additions to or alterations in the items in the tariff. I can tell my hon. friend that in connection with many items the rates provided for in the present agreement are below what was being charged on United States goods under the budget of May 1, 1930. However, that would be an inaccurate generalization if it were taken to be true all through. There are cases where it does not apply. While I think a great deal of the budget of 1930 and its proposals applied to conditions prevailing at that time, I would not say that in connection with every item I would be inclined to do the same thing in view of the conditions which apply in 1937. I have tried to view the matter objectively and deal specifically with each item in accordance with the conditions that prevail to-day, having regard to our trade situation.
My hon. friend must remember that in 1930 the United States came under our general tariff, whereas under the agreement of a year ago it automatically came under our intermediate tariff with respect to all its exports to this country. That is a consideration which must enter in relation to the tariff schedules we are now discussing, particularly in relation to the marginal aspects of the matter as between the British rate on the one hand, and the intermediate rate on the other. I should like to make a few observations with regard to cotton seed oil, Mr. Chairman. I am sure the minister will agree that while it comes here from the United Kingdom the points of origin are Egypt and India, so when we consider this item in terms of trade perhaps we would be justified in short-circuiting England, Ireland and Scotland and getting right back to the point of origin, which in the main is India. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: From India direct?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is not affected by this item.

Let me get back to the point I was trying to make. If one should suggest any measure of consideration for the producers of animal oils and fats in Canada, in view of this tremendous importation of cotton seed oil, which in this one division

Canada-United, Kingdom Trade Agreement
amounts to 25,597,600 pounds-and the minister knows there are two other divisions- the thought would immediately come to one: Well, but we must not disturb our trade with the country originally producing the cotton seed. That country is principally India, and to a lesser degree China.
As I started to say a moment ago, we imported from India $8,245,000 worth of goods and exported $2,473,000 worth. Does the importation of this huge amount of cotton seed oil or other products of the cotton seed help the agricultural Englishman, Irishman, Scotsman or Welshman, or does it not rather help our friends in India, who grow the cotton? Our friends overseas, who the other evening were called sharp traders or shrewd traders or something like that, are the people who sit in their offices and pull the strings, bring the seed from India to England, press it and send the resultant oil to Canada to the extent of some 25,000,000 pounds. Does that trade actually help our fellow Englishman, Irishman or Scotsman, as the case may be, the individual agricultural worker or artisan, or does it rather help those large organizations who handle this business? That is the point I want to make, in order that in considering this item hon. members of the committee may start with the essentials and give some thought to the man who originally produces the material.
When this seed gets to England it produces fifteen per cent cotton seed oil, forty-five per cent mill feed which is fed to cattle and hogs in England, twenty-nine per cent hulls and five per cent cotton linters. The oil is shipped to Canada. It is a neutral oil, limpid and wholesome looking, which is treated with hydrogen gas to bring it to a consistency that will enable it to compete with a similar product which might be made in Canada from commodities we in this country should be able to produce.
I should like the committee to bear with me for five or ten minutes while I deal with the products I have in mind. We produce animal oils and fats in Canada, and we could produce a great deal more. I have an idea in the back of my mind that the white race needs animal fats. I have another idea in the back of my mind that in the years to come it will be proved that while the peoples of India and Africa, where the largest proportion of oils of this kind come from, may be able to live on vegetable oils, we in this country will be much better off if we stick to the product which a kind providence has given us in abundance in our own country for the strengthening of the white race as against the other races. We require a certain amount of fat to sustain life. I should like to read into
31111-121$
the record various opinions by medical men as to the amount of fat required by a human being in order to sustain himself. First I quote from a book published by Robert Hutchison, M.D., Edinburgh, F.R.C.P., physician to the London hospital and also to the children's hospital '' London, England; author and lecturer on medical subjects, entitled Food and the Principle of Dietetics. He says that the maximum which a human can consume each day is 150 grammes of fat. This can be absorbed daily without much difficulty, but with most persons anything above 100 grammes in winter or less than 100 grammes in summer would be apt to produce disorders of digestion. Many authorities, however, recommend that the daily ration of fat should not fall below 75 grammes.
McLester, the American author, in his book Nutrition and Diet in Health and Disease, quotes the eminent German authority Voit as prescribing 56 grammes or approximately two ounces of fat daily. Samson, another eminent and widely quoted United States authority, estimates that the human system consumes 100 grammes per day, or three and a half ounces. For easy figuring, and in order that members of this committee may understand the foundation I want to lay for my argument, suppose we make the daily average 100 grammes or 700 grammes per week. At 28i grammes to the ounce, that means approximately 25 ounces per week or, roughly, a pound and a half. One pound of that may be considered as being made up of straight fat, such as butter, oils and so on, and we may say that the other half pound is assimilated during the week in the consumption of pies, pastry, fried foods and so on. So we will say one pound of straight fat per person per week is required as a maximum. At fifty weeks in the year that would be fifty pounds per year per person. Ten million of our people using fifty pounds per year each, means that the Dominion of Canada requires
500.000.	000 pounds of fat in order to sustain
and maintain her people. I make this statement, that we Canadian people and particularly the agriculturists-and to them I address these	remarks-can produce in Canada
500.000.	000 pounds of fat each and every year to sustain our own people.
For fifteen years I have sat in the house and have heard the agriculturists talk-mostly about wheat, of course-and have heard them say that they are the backbone of the nation. If that be the fact, then the challenge I put up to the agricultural industry is this: If you are the backbone of Canadian industry and of Canada itself, then produce sufficient

Canada-United Kingdom Trade Agreement
fats in Canada to sustain and maintain our people. Five hundred million pounds are required. I am not going to stress butter.

That fat is animal fat, like the fat which comes from the suet of a steer. It is all animal fat. True, it is only three or four per cent out of the milk from the cow, but nevertheless I maintain that that is animal fat, and for all practical purposes is part and parcel of the fat requirements of Canada.
The dietitians from whose records I have quoted certainly say that butter fat is a good fat for this or any other people, and to a great degree is preferable to many of the vegetable fats which are coming into this country in increasing amounts. The bacon is coming. We will bring home the bacon, although we must say that in this project we do not seem to have much success. Before we reach the bacon let us deal with beef.
In the abattoirs under government inspection in Canada, we slaughtered in the year 1935 832,540 beef cattle, averaging 1,100 or 1,200 pounds in weight. In the farming centres, beef rings, small slaughter houses and uninspected institutions throughout the length and breadth of Canada we have a figure equal to that, making a grand total in the year 1935 of 2,035,698 head slaughtered in Canada. It is on record that each and every head of beef averaging 1,100 pounds will yield an average of 45 pounds of edible fat or tallow. Over and above that, in the inspected abattoirs we slaughter 589,066 calves and veal, and 897,314 head of sheep and lambs. The total of sheep and lambs slaughtered throughout Canada in uninspected and inspected abattoirs is 1,696,061. If we add the calves, the veal, the sheep, and the lambs we have another figure of about 2,000,000. Each lamb, calf or sheep will average five pounds of edible tallow or fat. You have 45 pounds from beef, and 5 pounds from sheep, lambs and calves, making a total of 50 pounds. Then, 50 pounds for
2.000.	000 head of stock gives a total of 100,000,000 pounds of edible fat. If we add that
100.000.	000 pounds to the 100,000,000 pounds of dairy butter and the 250,000,000 pounds of creamery butter, we now have a total of 450,000,000 pounds.
As the minister has said, we have not touched the bacon, or brought home the bacon. Only 50,000,000 pounds more is required to make up the total, and we have all the hogs to deal with. In the inspected abattoirs we slaughter 2,969,987 hogs, and adding the figure from the uninspected institutions we get a total slaughter of 5,415,289, or as is commonly said 6,000,000 hogs per year. A slaughtered hog produces 15 pounds of edible fat. With 6,000,000 hogs at 15 pounds each we have a total of 90,000,000 pounds. In our computation we already have 450,000,000 pounds if we add that 90.000,000 it will bring our total up to 540,000,000 pounds of edible fat available in Canada to-day to supply the requirements of the Canadian people. The amount required, according to the best authorities in dietetics, is barely 500,000,000 pounds. Therefore I make the statement that we can supply the edible fat requirements of our Canadian people.
I say at once that if your tastes demand vegetable oils of some kind or another, or cotton seed oil, and if you want to pay for them, by all means have them. If we take

Yes, "refined cotton seed oil"; let me finish my sentence. The average cost was less than six cents per pound. All right. Now, the minister has said that it is not imported for food, that it is inedible. I do not think he meant to say that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I just quoted the item.

But he knows, I know, and parliament should know that these products come into Canada and are indexed in this blue book as "not for food," when actually they are "for food." When those oils arrive here they are refined and sold throughout the length and breadth of this country as food. These statistics are compiled year after year and the Canadian people are hoodwinked into believing that these products are not being used for food. When you slaughter beef cattle you insist upon government inspection in the abattoirs, but on the other hand you permit tank steamer loads of these commodities to come into this country, labelled as being "not for food purposes," shipped without any inspection or control, and refined and sold as food to the tune of 103,000,000 pounds last year. That is what is going on.
How much was made in 1934?

Roughly about 82,000,000 pounds, and about 56,000,000 pounds in 1933. Back in the oleomargarine days when the Liberal party was in power the manufacture amounted to only 4,475,000 pounds. A cry went up to high heaven against these importations. Not only were the importations stopped, but the product could not be made in Canada. Since I have been in this house, that figure of 4,475,000 pounds has increased until in 1935 it reached 103,000,000 pounds. A good deal is going to be said about this before we are much older. The Minister of Finance must be made to feel that something should be done about it.
I want to make this point abundantly clear. Away back in the oleomargarine days when the manufacture amounted to only 4,475,000 pounds, a conference was held in Ottawa on May 30, 1923. The present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) was in the chair, and among those present were the Hon. G. P. Graham, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), the late Mr. Robb, the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell), Mr. Stewart and other hon. members. In order to save time I shall not give the prefixes and affixes to the names of all these gentlemen. The conference was considering this item,

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oleo.

Oleomargarine. It was decided to stop the blending of our animal fats with the vegetable fats from other countries in order to make oleomargarine. The figures I have given refer only to vegetable oils, such as cotton seed oil, and yet only thirteen short years ago the government of that day prohibited the use of Canadian materials in manufacturing this particular product.
While we are bringing in these large quantities of cotton seed oil, we are shipping out of this country quantities of butter and fats of all kinds. It is only a few years ago that provision was made for a bonus on the export of butter to the extent of $100,000. Yet we let this other oil come in free of duty. I ask hon. members to note the geography of this country. We are bounded on the south for 3,000 miles by a country with a population of well over 100,000,000. Hon. members will ask themselves, as I have asked myself: What are they doing? There is an administration in power in Washington which some people consider as being akin to the administration in power here. Even though the party in power in the United States do not like to be called protectionists, they realized the menace to their home industry and- they passed certain measures to the detriment of Canada. Our economic and industrial situation is similar to theirs. Their markets are our markets. Ever since Chicago has been a city it has been the fat market of the north American continent. It bears the same relation to Toronto as it does to New York.
What has the United States done during the last few years in connection with this tremendous flood of oils coming into their country? On June 21, 1936, they put an excise duty of three cents per pound against Canadian animal oils and fats. I wish the minister would use some of the good will which he radiates when dealing with these

Canada-United, Kingdom Trade Agreement
items in an effort to bring about some reciprocal treatment on the part of Washington. As I say, on June 21, 1936, the United States Congress passed what is known as the Bailey amendment. That amendment provided for a duty-I must not call it a duty; it was an excise duty-upon animal oils and fats. Democrat governments do not place duties upon commodities, they place excise duties against them. If hon. members can tell the difference between the two I wish they would let me know. Excise duties are provided for when the Democrats are in charge, and when the Republicans are in power tariff duties are provided for. In this case the excise duty was three cents per pound on animal products. There was already one-half cent per pound duty, so this made the total rate 34 cents and 44 cents per pound average on vegetable oils. In addition they passed section 702, which provided for a processing tax of 3 cents per pound on certain fats, and 44 cents per pound on the other group of fats. The result was that the commodities which we are now discussing were faced with a tax of 34 cents per pound in one case, 44 cents per pound in another: It was 5 cents per pound on cocoa-nut oil, which I shall deal with later, and 4 cents on peanut oil-I shall leave that until later.-when entering the United States from the countries to which I have just referred. They slowed down the importation into the United States of these products. They shut off Canada's normal exports of 30 to 50 million pounds of animal fats into the United States. They slowed down the imports from the world of a billion pounds of vegetable oils. Yet these world sources of supply have free access into Canada, with the result that we are finding the Canadian market demoralized, and before we are twelve months older the fat production of the farmers of Canada will have been so disastrously affected that something will have to be done. For the moment, due to the world armament situation and the fact that these fats produce from 10 to 13 per cent glycerine-and the glycerine market jumped from 6 cents eight or nine months ago to 22 cents in New York to-day- and there is 10 per cent glycerol in these products-there has been a world market firming of the price.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Of all of them?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, except butter.

And as I pointed out during the few remarks I had the pleasure of making in a previous debate, when this artificial stimulus which has been given to these

markets and affects them to-day starts to fade, what are we in Canada, an agricultural country, going to do about it? That is the position in which we find ourselves as regards this item. Seeing that we buy, as we do from India, one of the countries of origin, $8,900,000 worth of products and sell them only $2,000,000 worth, and recalling that the balance of trade with Egypt, the other producer of cotton seed in the hull, is against us, if some little thing were done to help the Canadian producer of fat products you would not be hampering freer trade. As long as you give a preference to the Englishman-and he is the man you are thinking about when you are dealing with this schedule-he is satisfied.
When this 10 per cent preference was provided, these goods were being treated in Germany, Denmark, France and the Netherlands, more particularly, but that preference diverted the trade to England, with the result that a normal pressing of only 1,300,000 long tons per year jumped to a volume last year of pressed nuts and seeds of all kinds of 1,870.000 long tons. The Englishman, then, is satisfied. As he expressed it to me during a conversation in 1932:	Give us a preference and we will get the trade. England is a workshop; the Englishman knows how to handle trade. Perhaps you and I, sitting in this house, think we are helping the English artisan or farmer. If I could think of a better word than manipulator I would use it; I would not want such an expression to go to my English friends overseas, but the man who operates that English plant by machinery employs but few men and handles millions of pounds of raw materials provided by the colonies.
Some of my friends ask:	Who in Canada
imports all this oil? Ninety per cent of it is imported by just five firms. I am going to mention their names. I realize that they are not here to protect themselves, but every word I say will be a word of congratulation and commendation for their conduct of their business. They know how to run their business, and if I commend and congratulate them I should not be condemned for mentioning their names.
Swift and Company. I do not need to say anything about where they come from or who they are. They are a very efficient organization.
Lever Brothers. A sizable portion of their business is the manufacturing and selling of edible oils to the trade. They have connections in England. They are a great credit to Canada, and an efficient organization if there

ever was one. We are glad to have them here. So we have one controlled in the United States and one in England.
Next, Proctor and Gamble, Hamilton "Crisco"-controlled, operated and run from Cincinnati. If you want to sell them anything, go down to Cincinnati as I have done. They are a high-class United States concern and deserve a lot of credit.
Then there is the Palmolive Company, promoters of that schoolgirl complexion you hear so much about, the Canadian organization being a branch of the United States organization.
There are four of the firms, and to what extent they are Canadian you and I may judge, but 1 say they are well organized, well run and efficient organizations, giving a great deal of work to our Canadian people, and we are glad to have them here.
Incidentally, if I may be permitted to interject a personal note-I have nothing whatever to do with any packing house, and at no time in my career have I had a dollar in one. Because my name happens to be Joe Harris I hope I shall not be confused with the Harris Abattoir Company. They are a great firm and a credit to Canada, and I know the men in charge, but I have nothing whatever to do with the organization, and never had. So any remarks I may make in this house are not coloured or influenced by the people with whom I have the pleasure of doing business, but are made primarily on behalf of the Canadian agriculturist. By making a speech of this sort on behalf of our agriculturists I take some risk of not being reelected in a city constituency. If I was speaking with sole regard to my position as representative of a city constituency, they might want cheap oil so that the poor people could get cheaper products with which to maintain themselves.
Fifth, Canada Packers. Canada Packers is a great credit to Canada. It is a wonderful thing that Canadians have built up such an organization as this to process products produced by our people on behalf of our people. Criticize them as you will; I still say they are a great credit to Canada.
This little group of five firms imports
25.000.	000 pounds of cotton seed oil and
60.000.	000 pounds of palm oil, and so on all down the line, and I venture the opinion that by April 1 of this year there will have been imported into this country 250,000,000 pounds of these products. The minister says, mark you, they are not for food; but I venture the opinion that 125,000,000 pounds are brought in for no other purpose but to be refined and made into products that will be sold in Canada for food, and sold, as I said a while ago, with
very little inspection by the Minister of Agriculture, who 1 observe has retired one seat further back. He knew about this situation last May. He has known about it for some years. But he is so wheat-tweet-tweet-minded that I am afraid he cannot get a little oil into his system. I recommend that he get a little into his system.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Vegetable oil?

I recommend some good stearine. This is a serious problem for Canada. The price structure alone is something that we should give consideration to. If you take this 25,000,000 pounds of cotton seed oil and turn it into a product that can be used, say for shortening, do you not replace butter? You say you do not replace butter, you do not replace lard, you do not replace beef dripping. I say that you do replace these commodities. I sent a little clipping to the minister. Here is a baker in Hamilton using 100 per cent butter for his shortening-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And is sufficiently unique to boast about it.

That is right; that is important. I appreciate that, coming from the minister; and perhaps there is some line of argument in the back of his mind right now. Perhaps he would suggest that more should be done in the direction of producing our own Canadian products. But I say that we have to face the situation where we have
25,000,000 pounds of cotton seed oil coming in at 5-7 cents per pound, and we have to ask ourselves this question: How is the man who is collecting milk from cows yielding Zi per cent butter fat to compete with a product of that kind? That product is dumped on the St. Lawrence river from a tank freighter through a six inch pipe line and it competes with the products of 40,000 dairy farmers in Saskatchewan. That is the unhappy position in which providence has placed us; and providence will say to you if you ask him about it, "God helps those who help themselves." I say that the time has come for us to help ourselves in this particular problem.
The minister closed his speech the other night with a reference to the consumer. If something is being done, either by a processing tax or by an excise tax or by a duty to help out the situation, I can imagine my hon. friend opposite-I have forgotten his constituency, but he knows whom I mean-saying that the cost to the consumer is going to rise. Cotton seed oil was the first product to be denatured of its odour and peculiar taste and made into a limpid, odourless, tasteless, one hundred per cent oil. This was accomplished in 1887 by the Wesson process, which

Plus the tariff.

So I appeal to the Minister of Finance. He will probably be going to England and sitting in at a conference. We do not want to make this a political question in any sense of the word- I do not say to get a laugh from my friends opposite-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: First I want to congratulate the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris) on his excellent presentation of a case which he has presented) to me previously. It is always worth while to hear a man talk who knows his own business thoroughly and can explain it.
Will the minister permit me? If he will just take out that word "own" business-say the business.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I always understood my hon. friend to be engaged generally in the business which he has been discussing.
Well, to a degree, probably 5 or 10 per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not mean to imply that my hon. friend's argument was one of self-interest, and I am sorry if I gave that impression. But that he is a specialist in connection with this class of business he has demonstrated. I was really paying him a compliment. I also accept what he said as to the non-political nature of his remarks.
Do not be so sure of that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, I may tell my hon. friends behind me that I am sure of it because the party to which the hon. member for Danforth belongs was in power for five years, during the whole of which time these vegetable oils from the British Empire remained free. I am quite sure-my hon. friend will correct me if I am wrong-that he made the same kind of speech in committee of ways and means back in 1932 as he made to-day. I hope he is not going to fall from grace by saying this is the first time.
I do not like to interrupt, but if the minister will permit me, he knows and I know that this matter was not brought to a head until the United States took certain action in June, 1936.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But the imports of vegetable oils into Canada were very considerable.
And I made a speech on it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As far as the competitive effect on Canadian animal fats is concerned that effect has been present for some time, although the increased* imports in recent years indicate that if there is any effect, that effect has increased. I admit that in the short time I have been Minister of Finance I have had a
1928	COMMONS
Canada-United. Kingdom Trade Agreement
great deal of difficulty with animal fats. My hon. friend and other hon. members of the house and some people outside who are interested] have done a pretty fair job in organizing public opinion with respect to their views on the matter. I am not blaming them for it; that is their right, but I do feel a little concerned over the fact that this sort of thing starts and becomes such an. enormous problem overnight soon after a Liberal government comes into office. That is the only political word I intend to say; from now on I want to talk about the facts as I know them.
The animal fat producers of Canada, not including the dairy people, made representations to me something over a year ago with respect to the action of the United States in barring exports of animal fats from Canada to that country, the action not being directed against Canada particularly but being taken for the reasons indicated by the hon. member for Danforth. In that connection my attention was directed by my hon. friend from Danforth to Canadian consumption of products of this kind and to the increasing competition of vegetable oils. I think I am correct in saying that at that time my hon. friend was engaged in making a detailed study of the effects of those importations, the results of which he has given to the committee tonight. I want to emphasize, however, that at that time there was in my mind no idea at all of the competition of these vegetable oils with our dairy products, and I do not think my hon. friend had then reached the conclusion that they were at all a serious competitor with dairy products.
Well, I went to England to negotiate this treaty. Obviously the British people were interested in continuing free entry into Canada of a commodity such as this which, from their point of view, was an important export commodity. The fact that they import the raw material from India or Egypt does not lessen their desire to obtain a market for the refined product they derive from that material, and I did not offer any great difficulty in agreeing to continue free entry of these vegetable oils, not merely those included under this item but also those dealt with in the three or four succeeding items.
It is a little difficult to generalize about them, but I am sure my hon. friend will admit that some are positively not edible and cannot be refined to make them edible. My hon. friend spoke of the Wesson process in connection with cotton seed oil, but the Wesson process is not equally effective with respect to some of the other vegetable oils which are imported in large volume, and which by no stretch of the imagination can be said to

come into competition with dairy products, though of course all these importations are in greater or lesser degree in competition with animal fats as distinguished from dairy products. I drew then, and I still draw a distinction between the product of the cow while she is living and the product of the cow after she is dead. The dairy product is distinguished in all our minds, I am quite sure, from the product of the beast after it has been killed.
The fat is a factor whether the animal is dead or giving milk.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Undoubtedly it is a factor, but I think my hon. friend from Dufferin-Simcoe will admit that in this connection our dairy products are of more importance to us than the animal fat residue of the beast after it is killed.
I am not so sure about that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I hold that view very strongly, because fifty pounds is the beginning and the end of it as far as the animal fat content is concerned, while on the other hand during the productive life of the animal she produces three and a half pounds of butter fat per hundred pounds of milk.
The lady has a brother, sir.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Certainly; some ladies
have brothers, but in any case the brother does not produce milk or butter fat. However that may be, after I returned last fall my hon. friend brought a delegation to see me on this question. And lo and behold, for the first time there appeared as part of that delegation representatives of the National Dairy Council of Canada, who wanted me to consider the relationship of this question to dairy products and butter. That was the first occasion on which the question of a tariff on vegetable oils had been related to the butter argument. Up to that time, as my hon. friend will agree, I had discouraged a reference to the tariff board. On that delegation, as I say, there were the dairy people and some of the packers. You see, of course, it depends entirely upon what class of business the packers are in, as to the stand they take in this connection. Naturally there were not on the delegation headed by my hon. friend from Danforth representatives of the packers who were importing this material.
Not headed by me, but by a gentleman from Montreal. I trailed along.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Well, yes; the hand was the hand of Jacob, but the voice was the voice of Esau. Naturally none of the packers

named by my hon. friend as importers of vegetable oils were represented on that delegation, but several other packers were. Apparently it does not depend on whether or not you are a packer; it depends on what kind of packer you are and just what sort of business you are in whether you are on the side of the question represented by my hon. friend from Davenport and those with him, or on the other side. Were any representations made by the pilchard oil industry? That would be in competition also.

I cannot recollect any
at the moment, though there may have been some a year ago. I have received thousands of communications in this connection, of course. I am inclined to think that my hon. friend from Danforth and those associated with him may feel that I was scarcely frank with them in agreeing to that reference to the tariff board when on behalf of the government of Canada I had already undertaken with the government of Great Britain that free entry of these oils from Great Britain should be continued. I now make the explanation, and I hope an apology will not be necessary. It was not possible for me as a minister of the crown, knowing what I knew, to communicate that information at that time to interested parties who were waiting on me in connection with the matter. My hon. friend may ask: Well, if you had already made an arrangement with Great Britain why did you give us the reference to the tariff board? The answer is that I thought the reference to the tariff board would bring out all the information.
I may point out also that what we are considering here to-night involves not only free entry under the British column, but also a ten per cent duty against intermediate countries. There is nothing in the agreement to prevent us from increasing the intermediate and general rates at any future time if in the judgment of the parliament of Canada that should be a desirable thing to do. For that reason I thought the people interested had the right to a reference to the tariff board, and they got it. However, I could not communicate to them at that time, as I say, that the British agreement contemplated a continuance of free entry.

Could the minister tell
us, just to illuminate the discussion, what proportion of the imports comes in under this item, and what proportion under the intermediate rates?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will have to give it
under each item separately, and I shall do it later. I could not even approximate it at this time. I may say, however, that at present the imports are unimportant from intermediate countries, because prior to 1932 these oils were Tree wherever they came from. In 1932 British oils were left free, and hon. members opposite imposed a duty of ten per cent against all other countries.

At the request of Great
Britain.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Possibly at the request
of Great Britain; I do not know. I have no knowledge of what effect an increase in the intermediate duty might or might not have. That is one of the points on which I thought possibly we might get information from an examination by the tariff board.
My point in telling this history I am now about to make. It became public, of course, that the Minister of Finance had granted a reference to the tariff board with respect to vegetable oils coming into Canada. The board gave it wide publicity, and invited the public and those particularly interested to come to give evidence. What resulted? I will tell the committee, just to show that there is another side to this question. No less than sixty members of this house-more than sixty-wrote me protesting against any idea of putting a duty on these imported vegetable oils, and conveying to me resolutions by the hundreds from all the bakers in their constituencies, from all the laundry people in their constituencies, and from others interested in the use of this commodity. I repeat, there were no less than sixty members, regardless of .party. In fact, I believe there are members in the committee to-night who will remember communicating to me the most violent kinds of protests from people in their constituencies engaged in these different classes of business who claimed they would be ruined if a duty were put on vegetable oils, as was proposed by the applicants in the hearing before the tariff board.
I thought a storm had been raised. I have no doubt the hon. member will reply, and probably accurately, that this was the result of propaganda from those interested in keeping oils free of duty on entering Canada. But I assure him I doubt very much if there is a

baker from Sydney to Vancouver who did not address a letter to me, in addition to those I received from members of the house who wrote me about the matter.
I did not write you, honourable sir.
Nor did I.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend is an exception; I think he must have been away on a holiday. Then, there were not only bakers but-	[DOT]
Half-bakers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
-users of soap, soap powders and that sort of thing, who wrote me. Quite a number of people keeping stores and interested in the sale of packaged shortening, wrote protesting. The hon. member for Danforth, and those who believe with him, got busy. They saw the result of propaganda, and evidently thought it would be well to try it. Since they started I have been in receipt of literally hundreds of communications from dairy organizations from one end of Canada to the other who are inclined to think the hon. member is right, and that unless something can be done to stop vegetable oil coming in some horrible end awaits the dairy cow, that it will put the Canadian cow out of business.
There the situation stands. There the issue is joined between those who are using the commodity and who believe they will be seriously injured if a duty is put against it, and, on the other side, those producers who have been convinced by the hon.. member for Danforth and those associated with him that unless a duty is put against the commodity their interests will be prejudicially affected.
May I express my own views in the matter, so far as they have gone? In doing so I do not wish to prejudice the report from the tariff board which I hope to receive, but which I am assured by the chairman will not, due to the complexity of the question and the voluminous nature of the evidence both pro and con, be presented for some time. Speaking subject to that qualification, my own view is that it is conceivable that the growing importance of vegetable oils may have effects which even up to now could not be foreseen. The hon. member for Danforth has mentioned one factor which has a bearing in the opposite direction, namely, the factor of increased prices for vegetable oils in countries which are arming. That increase comes about because of the glycerine content contained in them. That may have -what might be described as a mitigating effect upon their competitive relation to our Canadian production of animal

fats. I am not yet prepared to admit, I am not yet convinced, and have not had the evidence to satisfy me, that the present importation of vegetable oils is at all a serious competitor of the Canadian dairy cow in her productive capacity. I am willing to admit they compete with her after she is dead, but I have yet to be shown that they are a serious competitor with her so long as she is alive. However, as the hon. member for Danforth knows, I am willing to be convinced.
Now, have I said sufficient, together with the informative address of the hon. member for Danforth, to show the committee what a difficult and complex question this is, and that it will repay close and unprejudiced examination by producers and consumers in Canada, because obviously to a very large measure it affects both classes?
I was a little amused, may I say, to get from some twenty members of the house, and from others outside the house-letters on both sides of the question. When the bakers and laundrymen were busy, I got rather warm letters from them telling me that on no account must a duty be put on these articles. Then later, when the dairy associations and others got busy, I got further letters, including those from the same twenty members, telling me that a duty must be put on these articles-all of which leads me to think that there is quite a number of members in the house who require to balance themselves very carefully as between producers and consumers, in regard to this particular item.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: You are not keeping any secrets.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, I am not keeping
any secrets at all. But let me assure everybody that nobody will ever know the names of those members. I wished to give the information only in order to illustrate to the committee the difficulty of reaching a fair conclusion in a complex matter. I do not recognize necessarily that it is a tariff problem, but rather that it is an economic problem affecting our welfare.

I do not intend to speak at length. As the Minister of Finance has said, we have had a most excellent explanation of the issue by the person who understands it possibly better than any other hon. member. In making that statement I do not reflect at all upon the Minister of Finance. I am not surprised he has not yet made up his mind what he would do, especially after receiving recommendations from twenty hon. members whose names he will not reveal, who have advised him both ways.
