speechtext:
Is the
hon. member one of them?

No. I can say to the Minister of Justice that purposely I have been rather quiet this session, but at least I have not yet said yes and no to the same issue. I do not propose to add anything to the exhaustive explanation of the hon. member for Danforth, but as one interested in the live stock industry and in Canadian agriculture I do say that the Minister of Finance might say to me even more than to the hon. member for Danforth that I am speaking about my own business. I know he did not mean it in that sense, as he explained. The hon. members of this committee who should be the most concerned about this item are those who are themselves interested in or are the representatives of agriculture. I do not care whether they come from the far west or the extreme east; if they represent agriculture in this parliament it behooves them to consider what is involved in this issue. I do not propose to interject what might be termed a political slant, but if the next three years reveal a development similar to that which has taken place in the last three, it will strike almost a death blow to Canadian agriculture. I think the Minister of Finance will agree with me when I say that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would not go that far.
If the minister will not go that far, will he say that there will be no bad effect if our importations increase in the next three years as they have increased in the last three?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend is referring to edible oil. I do not think either he or I can make a positive statement at this time as to what is edible and what is not.

I quite agree. With the lack of inspection which we have had in this country, neither you, Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Danforth, nor myself could state to what extent these oils are edible or not. As one who knows something about the cost of producing animal fats and oils, I can say that they are very costly to produce. Every hon. member within sound of my voice will agree with me when I say that what this country needs more than anything else to make agriculture profitable, to ensure the stability of agriculture, to keep the land in western Canada from drifting away and to keep the land in eastern Canada fertile enough, is increased live stock production. I am not going to impose on hon. members a repetition of the remarks I have made on
other occasions. At different times I have attempted to convince my hon. friends from western Canada of the necessity of reasonable protection for the live stock industry of this dominion, in order that there may be more of a balance between the grain growers and the live stock producers.
When, the hon. member for Danforth and the Minister of Finance were speaking I attempted to figure out the cost of producing animal oils and1 fats. Perhaps I could put it this way. I attempted to figure out how much of the surplus products of this country would be consumed in the production of animal fats and oils. The hon. member for Danforth suggests, and I have reason to believe he is not far astray, that upwards of half of the vegetable oils being imported into Canada are edible. The Minister of Finance admits that whether or not they are edible, whether or not they are substitutes for butter fats, whether or not they are used only by soap manufacturers and so forth, they (io take the place of animal oils and fats which might be produced' in this country. It would take 150,000,000 bushels of the best hard wheat of Canada to produce the animal oils and fats to the equivalent of the vegetable oils being brought into this country.
This is a very important issue, and as a representative of an agricultural district and as a farmer I want to urge upon the Minister of Finance that he give it his most careful consideration because it is a dangerous issue. I can imagine that in three years time we may be bringing into this country considerably more of these products than we are bringing in to-day. We have increased our importations every year for the last three years. Mr. Chairman, before you more or less relinquished your political leanings, when you belonged more or less to one side of this house, you and I differed with reference to the necessity for protection for our live stock products. May I point out to you that prior to 1930 we were importing an enormous quantity of live stock products. Between 1920 and 1930 we saw an unbalancing of the agricultural production of this country. In 1920 or 1921 we were exporting more nearly the same quantities of live stock products and wheat than we have ever done since.
The live stock industry of Canada is undoubtedly the basis of Canadian agriculture. For many years this industry has produced even more than the grain growing industry, despite the millions of bushels of grain which have been grown in western Canada. In 1920 we exported from this country $77,000,000 worth of animal products. The government of that day, still clinging to the idea of freer

speechtext: You are starting something now.
If the Minister of Finance lets this go for three years he may be starting something.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

Then when my hon. friend came to this house he certainly misrepresented his position. We certainly had the understanding that he was a free trader. However, I do not wish to confuse the issue by interjecting tariff matters. I hope the Minister of Finance will give me credit for being sincere in this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Do not speak for me,
though.

I have not in the past and I do not expect I shall in the future. But tariffs are necessarily involved in this issue and I do not see why my hon. friends should hold up their hands in holy horror because mention is made of the tariff policy of this country. No party has condemned it more when in opposition and practised it more when in power than the Liberal party. This policy has become the policy of both parties to a great extent. I want to point out that at a time in 1930 when our grain elevators were filled with unsold wheat we were importing into this country vegetable products to the equivalent of 25,000,000 bushels of our wheat, in the form of animal fats and oils. Every farmer within sound of my voice knows that you cannot produce animal fats and oils with timothy hay; every farmer in the house knows that you have to feed costly grains. It 
is true that our farmers have struggled along for several years; it is true that between 1930 and 1935 there was a world depression; the farmers of this country have struggled through all these years. And now, when there is an opportunity for some improvement in live stock products, the farmer, with grain prices as they are, can scarcely make it pay to produce animal fats and oils; he would be better off to sell his hard grain. I again point out that in the production of animal fats and oils, live stock products, dairy butter if you will, lies the hope for the future of Canadian agriculture. There is not one capable business man in this house who will not have the reasons immediately in mind. I do urge upon the minister to think of these articles as an agricultural product. We are importing now the equivalent to the production of 150,000,000 bushels of grain if it was converted into animal products sufficient to produce the equivalent in oils and fats.
Is that in oils?
In fats and oils.
How many pounds of animal fats would 150,000,000 bushels of wheat produce?

I am speaking of the amount of animal fats which is gained as a by-product from the production of that amount of grain. I understand the Minister of Finance figured on the production of the total pounds. I am talking of fats and oils that are taken from the production we might have in this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Let me get this clear, please. Does my hon. friend mean that if we fed 150,000,000 bushels of wheat we should thereby produce enough cattle at the rate of 50 pounds of fat per head to equal the imports of vegetable oils?
It would amount to more than that on that basis. I was taking it on the hog production.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend will of course see what a fallacious basis that is.

I might point out that we have lost markets overseas which we should have saved and developed. I do not blame it all on one government; I have criticized in this house both governments for their neglect of markets overseas. In 1920 we sold more bacon than we have ever sold since. Not even with the imperial trade agreements, of which my party is proud, have we recovered in the British market the bacon trade we had in 1920. I wish to emphasize that the vegetable oils we are importing are

replacing to a great extent the oils and fats whose production through the live stock industry means a great deal in the stabilization of Canadian agricultural prosperity. I do not wish to derive any political advantage from this issue. I know that my friends to my right thought we overemphasized the importance of the importation in 1930 of New Zealand butter; the ex-Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) humorously remarked on different occasions that his government slipped out of power on New Zealand butter. I think it is only fair for me to say that I do not wish this government to slip out of power on vegetable oil, but-[DOT]
You want to slip in on it.

-I do urge the minister to keep an eye on the benefits which might be reaped by the Canadian agriculturist at a time when he needs them most. To my friends in western Canada may I say that we cannot produce animal fats and oils, whether in Saskatchewan or in Ontario, without consuming a great deal of hard grain which on many occasions is difficult to dispose of. I think there is 'here a very close relationship which should be carefully considered by the government of the day. I feel that I should express to the Minister of Finance my views as a farmer, and not wishing to delay the committee further I urge upon him the most careful consideration of this matter before he disposes of an issue which to my mind is vitally correlated with the future security of agriculture. The live stock industry is the basis of agriculture in Canada, as in every other country in the world.

Does it make any difference from what country cotton seed comes out of which this oil is produced in Great Britain? That is to say, are all importations of cotton seed oil from Great Britain made free under this agreement?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Continued free.
Are they continued free under this agreement no matter from what country the cotton seed itself comes?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Of course it makes no difference in what British country they originate. With respect to the importation of the seed itself into Great Britain from foreign countries, it would have to conform to the 50 per cent content provision of the agreement.
Is any inquiry made as to the source from which this cotton seed comes?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris) was quite right. It is principally India, and to some extent Egypt. I made some reference in the budget speech to our situation as regards India. While the privilege of the British rates in this agreement automatically extend to all countries of the British commonwealth, as my right hon. friend will remember, there is under the law power in the government by order in council to withdraw that privilege from any British country which does not reciprocate on a fair basis by way of trade agreement with Canada. As my right hon. friend knows, no government of Canada in recent years has been able to make a trade agreement with India, and as the hon. member for Danforth pointed out, the balance of trade between Canada and India is very heavily in favour of India-made up largely of tea and rice, and to some extent of many other commodities. It is the desire of this government, as I believe it was of the previous one, to reach a trade agreement with India; and in that regard one does not forget, of course, the power which the government has to withdraw from India or from any other British country the privilege of British preferential rates unless it is possible to reach a fair trade agreement with her. I am not now issuing any warning or anything of that nature to India, but it is well that we should see facts.
Unless India reciprocates in a way that is satisfactory to this country, the government would have the power to withdraw this privilege with reference to their cotton seedi; is that right?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My right hon. friend will understand that in the case of cotton seed, which comes from India to England and is there processed, the situation of that product for content purposes would be affected by any action which we might take vis a vis India.
Is the main reason why these empire products come to Canada via Great Britain that they should be processed there?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, they are the greatest processors of all.
That is the main reason they come via Great Britain?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Oh, yes, practically the only reason. As my hon. friend knows, England is the great gathering and distributing centre, particularly for these tropical products in which she has specialized for so

many years. There is no doubt that vegetable oils are supplied by Great Britain to most of the world, she being the country importing the seeds or nuts, as the case may be, and the pressing being done there for many countries, even outside of the British Empire, because they were first in the field, first saw the possibilities of it, and are in addition, of course, the great merchants of the world.

This is in no sense a political question. This item was made free by the Conservative government under the agreement in 1932, and now it is proposed to continue that free entry for another three years. As a matter of fact, though, the situation has changed tremendously. The minister himself has referred to the fact that the import of these oils has increased- from year to year during the last four or five years. He says we could not help that. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) yesterday or the day before told us that providence was with the government and that he would rather have it with them than against them. In this particular instance providence has been against the government, for during their term of office the importations of this oil have increased by leaps and bounds.
I represent an agricultural and dairy constituency, and I can assure the committee that no better herds are to be found anywhere in Canada than those in Argenteuil, so this is a matter that greatly affects the dairy people of that district. I have listened attentively to what has been said to-night, and though I .rave never given the subject much consideration before, I must say that I am impressed yy the argument put forward by the hon. member for Danforth. I believe the minister nimself is impressed by it. As a matter of fact this is a question of the utmost importance to the agricultural and dairy people of Canada and I urge the minister to consider it as carefully as possible, to go into it more fully, and let the tariff board make its report on this phase of the matter as well as on the importations under the intermediate and general tariff. Let the board make a full report on the question.
Under present conditions, though we want to trade with our friends in India, if they do not reciprocate in a way that is satisfactory to the government I suggest that we might very well consider the desirability, almost the necessity, of taking action under the powers which this government has to stop these vast imports of cotton seed oil made from cotton seed coming from India or any other country that does not reciprocate with us. I under-

stand that Canada will be bound for three years under this agreement. That cannot be helped; but I take it there will remain a residue of power in the government to take some action, not to prohibit import of these oils but to limit it to a reasonable quantity so that our agriculturists and dairy farmers may have a better chance to sell their products in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are now really discussing cotton seed and crude cotton seed for the manufacture of meal and refined oil. That particular product does originate in India and comes via the United Kingdom. But the difficulty to which my hon. friend from Danforth refers is only to a small degree created by imports of cotton seed oil. The total imports of cotton seed oil last year were less than a million and a half dollars. I am coming more and more to the view that the separation of edible and non-edible oils in a proper manner might go a long way towards the solution of the problem. I will not debate this question further because it is under investigation, and the tariff board reference covers all aspects of the question.
No objection has yet been taken to the importation of nonedible oils except those that can be refined into edible oils.
Could there not be one rate for edible oils and another for non-edible oils?

I am sure that everyone who has discussed the matter approaches it from the same standpoint, namely, the necessity and desirability of doing what we can to assist agriculture in Canada. We all know that during the last six or seven years agriculture has been passing through one of its most serious phases, and whether you consider it from the standpoint of the grain producer or the live stock producer or from any other point of view that is true. It has been necessary to give bonuses and to impose duties with a view to protecting agricultural products, and the argument that is made by the hon. member for Danforth, who has presented the case to-night, is along that line. There is no doubt that conditions have changed with respect to the importation of these commodities in the last few years. As I understand it, these products were free from Great Britain; they have always been free, there being no tariff against them. But the imports from any source were insignificant until within the last three or four years. There cannot be any question that the quantity of these oils imported has become a factor

Canada-United, Kingdom Trade Agreement
in connection with agricultural production. They are taking the place of animal fats, and that is in a measure beyond what could have been anticipated.
The minister has stated.' his position quite frankly. An agreement has been entered into covering a period of four years, but there is in that agreement a provision, article 16, which I think the minister and the government might make use of. It reads:
In the event of circumstances arising which in the judgment of the government of the United Kingdom or of the government of Canada, as the case may be, necessitate a variation in the terms of this agreement, the proposal to vary those terms shall be the subject of consultation between the two governments.
That is an elastic provision, and as the minister knows, since the agreements were first negotiated, advantage has been taken of it and concessions have been made in both directions. I suggest that when the facts are known in connection with the matter under investigation by the tariff board an opportunity will be afforded the minister to take the matter up in the light of the information he has, and to make representations under this article. We may talk about the agricultural industry, but after all dairying has been over the years the backbone of that industry, and the dairy cow needs all the help she can get, dead or alive. I am sure the minister appreciates the importance of this and. will give it the consideration it deserves in the light of the expansion of the competition of these oils with dairy products and animal fats. I hope he will deem it necessary to take action with a view to reducing this competition, which has not been foreseen, but which is growing and is likely to become quite serious. After all, the minister must be able to find a way out.

I am sorry I was not in the house earlier in the evening when the hon. member for Danforth began his discussion of the question. I did hear him, however, the other night when he referred to the subject in his speech on the budget, and I am sure that anyone who heard or read that speech could not help feeling something of the seriousness >f this menace-shall I say?-to our agriculture.
The value of these trade agreements lies largely in the benefits which they have brought and will continue to bring to the live stock and dairy industry of Canada. I doubt whether the government would have gone as far as they have by way of concessions to the British people in our markets if it had not been for the advantages we received in the entry of our dairy and hog and cattle products
into the British market. Therefore it seems too bad that this item has been left unchanged. The minister in his explanation to-night said that when the agreement was made he did not anticipate that the entry of these vegetable oils into Canada would have any effect whatever upon the dairy industry, but I think he and the committee will agree that when 103,000,000 pounds of edible fat and1 shortening is imported into Canada during the year, or made in Canada from imported oils, it must to a certain extent displace some kind of animal fat produced in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not necessarily. I cannot go that far.
Well, the greater part must displace some kind of animal fat.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: To clarify my point, I call attention to this fact: There is no question that animal fat shortening cannot be packaged and sold retail because it lacks keeping qualities. I am advised that a large business has been developed in packaged shortening, with vegetable oil as its base, which will keep on the store shelves. That is the point I had in mind when I said that there are some factors which require to be examined' in regard to competitive effects before I would accept the large figures my hon. friend mentioned.

I agree with what the minister has said regarding the keeping qualities of vegetable oil shortenings in packages. I admit that lard and shortenings of that kind probably will not keep as well as vegetable oil products, but before vegetable oils were in common use in this country the only alternative the Canadian housewife and people had was animal fat for shortening and similar uses. So I think my contention is fairly sound that these vegetable oils which are being brought in do to a certain extent displace the products of the Canadian dairy farm and live stock industry.
The dairy industry is a very important one for Canada. It brings larger returns to agriculture than any other branch of animal husbandry. The unfortunate thing is that we have a small exportable surplus. That small surplus of -milk or milk products is the dominant factor in determining the price of dairy products in Canada. If our dairy products and animal fats are to continue to be displaced in larger and larger amounts as time goes on, the result will be that we shall have a larger exportable surplus to go on the British market or wherever we can sell it.
We have heard from different parts of the house during the budget debate, and I have heard hon. members on both sides -make the

1936	COMMONS
Canada-United Kingdom Trade Agreement
statement in other places, particularly in some of the committees of which I happen to be a member, that the agricultural industry as a whole is not in a good position. The prices Obtained are in many cases not commensurate with the cost of production. The dairy farmers, many of them, are not enjoying the prosperity they should. So when their production comes in competition with a cheaper class of product such as vegetable oil, the tendency is to keep the prices of dairy products down below what they would otherwise be.
I know that it is impossible at the present time for the minister to make any change in the present agreement, but I think he should seriously consider, and that he will have to consider seriously within the next year or two, the proposition made by the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Stewart) that this matter should be brought to the attention of the British government and some concession be arranged.

I think I should not let this item pass without making a few remarks on the importance of the issue at stake. Those of us who were born and raised on dairy farms in Ontario, as I am proud to say I was myself, cannot but be seized of the importance of a matter so far-reaching in its effects as the item now under discussion. When one calculates that in a riding such as I represent, the county of Peel, for the last recorded year the production of milk reached the enormous total of 87,000,000 pounds, one gets some conception of the importance of this item to the dairy industry. Those of us who were conversant with the issue prior to 1930 when large importations of butter from New Zealand found their way into the markets of Canada, know full well the effect which that had upon the dairying industry here.
In the part of Ontario from which I come, the whole milk industry is the most important branch. We provide a large proportion of the milk for the great metropolitan market of Toronto. One of the major problems, and one which is most pressing with the farmers in that riding, is that of surplus milk. There is scarcely a milk association meeting anywhere in the neighbourhood of Toronto or any of the large urban centres where this question of surplus milk does not arise year after year. One of the reasons why there is a surplus of milk is that the farmers seek the best and most convenient and most remunerative market for the product of the dairy cow. One cannot blame them for that. The fact is that the surplus milk which exists in such great quantities around Toronto must find a release through some channel, and one of the channels which I have heard suggested on many occasions, both when I was on the

farm and since I have left it, is that, if the price of butter, cheese and other dairy products were higher in proportion to the price of milk, many dairy farmers would find it profitable to leave whole milk production and go into other lines of dairying. So, as was so forcibly shown to-night by the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris) and others, it is a matter of much importance that the farmers and dairymen of this dominion should be seized of the grave consequences which come from the free entry of these oils competing with the product of the dairy cow. After all, it does not seem to me that we are likely to do much in the way of increasing the price of the dairy commodities which the farmers have to sell so long as we permit the competition of commodities produced under the conditions so clearly stated to-night by the hon. member for Danforth.
I often think that farmers do the least advertising of their products of any class in Canada. I am not referring, of course, to the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross) who is an excellent advertiser along certain lines. Someone just now suggests that he is not a farmer, but he has answered that point several times, and from his tremendous interest in wheat I am almost inclined to think that he must be engaged in some agricultural enterprise. In any event I do think that this vegetable oil industry, which produces the various brands of shortening and other vegetable oil products that are for sale in the country, very largely promotes the sale of those products through intensive advertising. I believe that this government, which from time to time spends money on things which it believes to be legitimate might give some consideration to spending some money in advertising our own agricultural products. The Minister of Agriculture looks very interested as he sits over there, and I am sure he would be the first to agree that wherever possible the products of the farm, particularly the dairy farm, ought to have some encouragement and assistance by way of advertising throughout the country. A couple of weeks ago I attended a little gathering at which I heard several housewives discussing vegetable oils in relation to the butter fat industry. An argument ensued, and it does appear to me that there is a grave division of opinion as to whether butter fat or vegetable oil is actually the best for the purposes of the housewife. I have come to the inescapable conclusion, however, that one of the reasons for the wide use of the different kinds of shortening is the extensive and intensive advertising which has been carried on.

Canada-United, Kingdom Trade Agreement
We are all interested in farm affairs and agriculture in general. It may be a hackneyed phrase, but agriculture is still the backbone of this country. If you study the matter at all you will soon find that when the purchasing power of the farmer is reduced there is not very much business left in the country for anyone else. So I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that our farm products ought to be brought before the purchasing public by means of intensive advertising. I think we have a right to expect that the purchasing public, not only in this country but overseas as well, should be made acquainted with the excellent qualities of the products of our farms.
I leave this suggestion with the Minister of Agriculture to-night. I think he might very well give some study to the situation, because in many instances the merits of our agricultural products are not being properly brought before that great buying public from which the farmer must obtain his livelihood.
Further, by way of caution to the Minister of Finance, I think we ought to be very careful to see that the interests of the dairy farmer in the province of Ontario, as well as in every other province of this dominion, are thoroughly protected against competition from products such as those which have been described and which are under discussion tonight, in order that the farmer of eastern Canada as well as the farmer of western Canada may receive a fair deal at the hands of the government of the day.

I should like to correct an observation made by the Minister of Finance, if I may, and in doing so may I say that I am very anxious that nothing that may be said by any hon. member of the 'house, particularly myself, shall prejudice our position before the tariff board.
The minister mentioned the name of the National Dairy Council of Canada, and intimated that he had received no word from them until they joined with the animal oil and fat producers. I am glad that the Minister of Agriculture is here. He knows, and the Minister of Finance knows, that the national dairy council make their representations to the Minister of Agriculture. They always cooperate and consult with the minister, and he and they get together and work out everything they possibly can in the best interests of Canadian agriculture. The Minister of Agriculture had representations made to him, and when those representations were made, I suppose the natural feeling was that they were being made to the government of 31111-122*
Canada. So when this is referred to as something new that was brought forward by this group of packers, if you like to call them that, who were not importing or manufacturing shortening, that is hardly the fact. I know that the first letter I saw in Montreal was written by the dairy council to the Minister of Agriculture, and I think as long as thirteen months ago he had certain people come to see him regarding the matter. If he will consult his files he will perhaps find correspondence from the hon. member for Chateau-guay-Huntingdon (Mr. Black), the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Davidson) and others, and he may remember that members of the dairy council had interviews with him and with the Prime Minister, who I am sorry is not here.
In all fairness I think the Minister of Agriculture should not let this item go through without giving us hi9 views based on the economics of this question, which I conceive to be of great national importance. Perhaps now that we are all tattling just a little, the Minister of Agriculture will remember that another member of this house, the hon. member for Danforth, discussed this matter with him and agreed that it was a matter for the Minister of Finance. The member for Danforth left the office of the Minister of Agriculture after that first interview, which was very cordial, and went to see the Minister of Finance. I do not propose to pursue the matter; I just wish to make the situation abundantly clear. The Minister of Finance rather left the impression in my mind that there might have been some deep-I will not say conspiracy, because that is not a nice word

but a correlation between the actions of certain groups, a getting together of strange bed-fellows all of a sudden to further their own interests.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I congratulated you on your organization, and1 I said so.

I will leave the Minister of Agriculture for a moment and deal with that point. Sixty members of parliament wrote letters as a result, as the minister knows, of propaganda by very powerful interests, carried on to the extent of many thousands of letters circularizing everyone on their lists of customers. They even went so far as to tell their members of parliament in writing, "Prices will jump four cents a pound immediately if the Minister of Finance takes any action on this question." That assertion is in black and white. I have it under my hand.

The evidence is available now to members of the house, or will be after the report of the tariff board is down. I do not wish to prejudice the position of anybody. But the bold statement was made, and the users and consumers, the bakers, confectioners, laun-drymen and so on swallowed it hook, line and sinker, and felt badly about it. Members of parliament were written to, but members of parliament -being such busy people just looked at it, and sent it to Mr. Dunning. So he got sixty letters. Had the other group which had been taking the Minister of Agriculture into their confidence, and now that their names have been mentioned I can name them-the National Dairy Council of Canada and the Animal Oil and Fat Producers of Canada-started out with propaganda, the minister would have had two complaints to-night, instead of one, from those members. The minister knows, and we know, that I had thought to keep this thing out of a political atmosphere. He will agree with me that neither the National Dairy Council of Canada nor the Animal Oil and Fat Producers permitted themselves to engage in any propaganda whatsoever in any way until after they felt the Minister of Finance was fully satisfied to air the whole thing.
The customers and friends of the five firms who control this business in Canada- two United States, one English, and one Canadian-had been spreading propaganda for months and had come here equipped with professors, statisticians, legal talent, and what not, to break down the issue as it was laid before the government by this other small group.
I had hoped that the problem being of such magnitude the Minister of Agriculture would have seen fit to confirm what I have said, that we worked through his department, or rather kept his department informed until such time as he thought it might be good business to approach the Minister of Finance on the problem.
Shall the item carry? Carried.
No; the Minister of Agriculture was on his feet.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
No, I was not on my feet; but I think in view of what the hon. member has said I had better check up on the records of my department. I realize the hon. member did come to my office on one occasion, and as he has already stated to the committee he informed me it was his intention to take this matter up with the Minister of Finance. In a very general way he outlined his ideas in regard to the matter, but did

not go into details. My memory is that all representations made to the department, so far as they were made to me personally, were pretty much along that line. The question was not discussed at length, but reference was made to the fact that they intended to bring the matter up with what they considered to be the proper department, the Department of Finance. But I should like to check up before making any general statement to the house on just what the records of the department are in regard to the representations made.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the Minister of Finance if, in view of the fact that this report will probably be down in a month or two, or three months, and in view of the fact also that these items are bound, is it still possible, as it was in the case of the previous agreement, to have conversations with representatives of -the United Kingdom, even on a bound item?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, on any item. That is covered by section 16 of the agreement. The parties to the -agreement reserve the right by agreement to vary its provisions.

The minister in making his earlier observations mentioned that there was that possibility. Is it the possibility he had in mind when on the budget speech being made he intimated the possibility of some amendments?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, it was a different thing altogether. In the budget speech I did not refer to the tariff items in the agreement. I referred to tariff board reports which might be received prior to this committee finishing its work. May I say that I have received some tariff board reports. I expect under the law to lay them on the table, but may I say that I should like to have a little -time to look into them before doing so. However, under the law I must lay them on the table within fifteen days of their receipt. Can we say " Carried "?
Carried.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Item agreed to.

Item 277.
Palm and palm kernel oils, unbleached or bleached, not edible; shea butter:	rate of
duty, free.
Carried.
Item 278.

Mr. Chairman, I do not take much of the time of the house. Further, I do not make any threats and do not purpose making any, but if you are going to start the practice of trying to carry items when I am on my feet-

Foreign Enlistment-Mr. Lapointe
I did not see the hon. member; I am sorry.

Perhaps you, Mr. Chairman, have been in the house long enough to-night to know that I have been talking on a matter of great moment to Canada, a matter respecting oil. Perhaps, you, sir, realize that the item previous to the one now called is of a like nature, that you have declared it carried, and have tried to get on with the next one.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In all fairness to the chair, if the hon. member will permit me, may I say that I am at least equally guilty, because the discussion in the last two and a half hours has ranged completely over the oil items. The observations of the hon. member were not confined to one item, and if he is insisting upon a strict interpretation of the rules, his remarks should have been confined to cotton seed. No one attempted to confine him to cotton seed. He was permitted, and I believe properly, to deal with the general question. I was under the impression that the discussion which we have had covered, not to the exclusion of further discussion, but to the satisfaction of the committee, items 277 and 278, at all events. However, I shall not insist. The committee can do as it likes, but it is my duty to point out-the hon. member said he did not want to threaten, and of course I am not threatening-that at the present rate of progress it will take six weeks of steady sittings to pass the items in the agreement. I speak only of the rate of progress, and move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again. Evidently it is not the intention to pass the oils items to-night.
Item stands.
Progress reported.
